topic: what needs to be added to players, teams, tactics and match engine to improve realism; starting point is the in progress plans

areas.name: The in-progress plans and what they miss
areas.brief: The engine workflow keeps its charter and sixteen slices. Realism runs as a separate programme after it, with its own performance budget. Core: realism bands are outputs, never tuning targets. Order: test harness, then team shape, then the event contract, then the season layer. Scope: twelve pieces routed to three design documents.

areas.name: The player as a person: attributes, personality, body, positions
areas.brief: A player becomes a person: a rating per position, a rating per foot, new performance attributes, twelve hidden personality traits, and learnable habits. Attribute effects are amplified beyond real sizes so quality is felt over about five matches. Personality is seen through scouting noise. Open: how the attribute and trait overlaps split in the engine.

areas.name: The club and the squad: identity, venue, mood, cohesion
areas.brief: A club has a style from identity, squad, and tactic, a home ground, a reputation, a squad familiarity per tactic, and a team mood that personality shapes. Style clash follows the measured additive possession rule. Open: none central.

areas.name: Tactics beyond Tier 2: phases, transitions, set pieces, live changes
areas.brief: Each team has an in-possession and an out-of-possession shape, set-piece routines, per-player and opposition instructions, and triggers. Live changes wait for the next stoppage, and both managers make them. Team shape and the block follow the measured slide with the ball. Open: the nine real phases against the two chosen.

areas.name: How the match plays: actions, choices, duels, the ball in the air, officials, injuries
areas.brief: Every action family resolves from the situation first and the player second. The duel is one contested action among several. Play in the air uses the ball height the engine already has. A full referee with a video assistant, and injuries with a severity. Open: three action families have no outcome evidence.

areas.name: The realism test: bands, design targets, watched reviews
areas.brief: The test bands measured per-match rates, scorelines, pass completion by kind, and joint spreads, with a real target and a design target where the game departs on purpose. People watch matches and seasons at milestones. StatsBomb and Transfermarkt stay, with the licence risk accepted. Open: none central.

areas.name: The manager as a modelled entity
areas.brief: Both managers are entities with attributes. The human's tactical attribute moves information accuracy, not instructions. The AI manager picks tactics from philosophy, opponent, match state, and season situation. Open: none central.

areas.name: The season layer: competitions, careers, market, club business
areas.brief: The season layer mirrors the European structure, with careers on per-attribute age curves, a market valued from visible data only, and a club business with a board and an owner. The fast model must pass the same season bands. Open: how development effects are sized, since no public data sizes them.

areas.name: The open questions the three design documents left (42 in all)
areas.brief: The forty-two open questions of the three design documents were closed in session six, except the technical questions of the event contract, which go to that build step's plan.

areas.name: The staff around the squad: coaches, scouts, medical staff, as people with their own quality
areas.brief: Every role a real club employs is a person with a rating that each club sees through its own judgment, full only in the active leagues. Advice can be wrong, overruling has a cost, staff can be poached, and staff set how fast tactics and routines are learned. Open: whose judgment rates staff.

areas.name: Contracts and the dressing room: negotiation, promises, agents, squad status, unrest
areas.brief: Contracts are negotiated by agent, director of football, manager, and family, and carry money, bonuses, clauses, and promises. The dressing room has standing, groups, a culture, and a view of the manager. Unrest escalates and has a small on-pitch effect. Discipline follows each country's rules.

areas.name: Supporters and the press: fan mood, expectations, interviews, media pressure
areas.brief: Supporters are groups whose balance is the fan mood, with power through the board, ownership models, money, and the manager. The crowd moves the referee and nervous players. Press conferences, journalists as people, and stories that build over weeks. Open: press duties by competition.

areas.name: International football: national teams, international breaks, call-ups, tournaments
areas.brief: The calendar, national teams, and players on duty are in the game; managing a nation comes later. Call-ups follow form, the coach's taste, loyalty, and depth. Duty brings fatigue, injuries with compensation, mood, and value changes.

areas.name: How the player watches the match: real time, key moments, other grounds
areas.brief: The player's match plays in real time or as tiered key moments, and the other matches run in the background with live scores. Open: most of the viewing design is only touched.

areas.name: New players entering the world: youth academies, youth intake, and generated players
areas.brief: Academies follow each country's structure, the full model starts at about 16, and a young player's future is a narrowing range. The generator copies measured patterns: birth quarters, late bloomers, national output. Style comes from where a player develops. Open: versatility and parent rates.

areas.name: The manager's week: information, time, team talks, and delegation
areas.brief: Team talks move mood and focus, delegation works the same in every area, and information arrives through an inbox, reports, and escalations. Open: how the manager's time is limited.

areas.name: The data model as an engine contract: attribute jobs, scale, visible and hidden, effective ability, role weights, sensitivity
areas.brief: Every attribute keeps a job; actions run in stages with blended, fitted weights. Tenths behind 1 to 20 for every rating in the game, a convex curve set by the five-match target. A bounded effective-ability layer, hidden values in words. About 40 roles with three behaviours. Team numbers act on team actions; identity acts off the pitch. Height, age, and adaptation act; build is a word. Relationships carry two numbers. A sensitivity test covers attributes, settings, roles, team numbers, and, over seasons, staff ratings. Core: all of it. Scope: keep all; eight design-document pieces are stale, to rewrite at the next distil.

areas.name: Action resolution and the probability layer: probabilities, shots, passes, duels, errors, variance
areas.brief: Each contact (tackle, first touch, keeper handling, strike, pass, interception) draws from the situation and the attributes; physics carries the ball between contacts. A strike takes two draws; a keeper's reach is physics and the handling a draw; penalties add a guessing game. Duels run in two steps with four outcomes. Errors come from draw tails, lapses, and named events. Checks: xG buckets by a real-data model, shot split, pass curves, duel set, Opta errors, and variance with real and design targets. Core: all of it. Scope: keep all.

areas.name: Machine load and save size: the cost of the realism additions on the player's machine
areas.brief: The game promises to run well on an ordinary laptop, with fixed limits the player feels and a relative limit per match in the tests. No realism lever is pulled; when the budget fails, engineering optimises first and comes back only if it still fails. Open: the limit numbers, for the plan.

areas.name: Realism calibration and validation: per-match targets, distributions, league tables, divisions, the harness
areas.brief: Targets from five recent seasons in three layers: per league with data, per tier, and banding groups for the rest; a division's style emerges from its players. Tolerance is the real spread plus sampling noise. Every scoreline and whole distributions are checked, and the league table in full. Each change runs a few thousand matches; each release a full run; every report is stored and compared. Leagues without data sit in banding groups fed by the tier formula. Core: all of it. Scope: keep all.

areas.name: Tactical counterplay and team-level AI: costs, counters, squad fit, shape, transitions, AI managers
areas.brief: Costs, counters, and squad fit emerge from play through the players, with no table and no fit number. Rest defence follows duties, and line gaps emerge. A round-robin of eight named styles runs on every change and a setting grid before release; every preset needs a clear weakness. AI managers use staff advice and memory, carry a scoutable fingerprint, and are checked for fit and the possession rule. Paired squads check fit. Beyond the brief: the AI learns in the match and an exploit hunt runs before release; players manage games with instructions on top; touchline shouts; conditions change which tactic works. Core: all of it. Scope: keep all.

areas.name: Match engine structure: two models, phases, pitch, clock, seeded replay
areas.brief: The full engine runs every active-league match; a fast model runs the rest, fitted from the full engine after each change and checked by season bands and per pairing. A written phase machine with a position check at each restart. Grounds differ in size within the laws. Added time prices each event kind, video reviews included. Replay is identical on every supported machine. Beyond the brief: a skip finishes on the fast model from the current state; background matches run first and reveal their events in step; every player thinks every tick; a mid-match save finishes on its old engine. Core: all of it. Scope: keep all.

items.text: The tactics-and-ai slice of the engine build carries a benchmark tripwire: it fails if CPU time per match rises more than 10 percent, or memory more than 25 percent, over the match-rules baseline.
The ball already carries a three-dimensional position and velocity, so height exists in the engine today and an aerial model has somewhere to live.

The referee is a full official, with a foul tolerance, a card threshold, how often the referee plays advantage, how consistently the referee applies that threshold, and a leaning towards the home side that the crowd can move.
items.why: Asked whether the referee is a character, the person took the fullest option: a full official with a home leaning.

items.text: Pitch condition and weather both exist and they interact, so rain on a worn pitch is worse than either one alone.
items.why: Asked whether conditions exist, the person took the fullest option: pitch and weather, interacting.

items.text: An injury carries a severity, and its risk comes from what happens in play (hard tackles, fatigue past a threshold, a collision) rather than from a flat chance per minute.
items.why: The person took the fullest option over binary injuries; driving risk from hard tackles also finally gives the aggression attribute a real effect.

items.text: The aerial model supports flight arcs, heading duels, goalkeeper claims, and spin and swerve, so a player's technique and preferred foot change where the ball ends up.
items.why: The person took the fullest option, using the ball height the engine already carries and that nothing yet uses.

items.text: The engine build's benchmark tripwire (10 percent CPU and 25 percent memory over the match-rules baseline) guards the engine build against its own baseline and stops there; the realism programme measures against the shipped engine and sets a performance budget of its own.
items.why: The realism programme should pick a budget it can live in rather than inherit one written for a different purpose.

items.text: A real match carries about 1683 events. Wyscout types them with 10 types and about 35 subtypes, Metrica with 9 types and subtypes, and kloppy's interoperable model with 19 types (measured over 1826 Wyscout matches from five leagues in 2017/18).

Pass completion depends on the kind of pass rather than on one rate: simple passes complete 91.7 percent, headers 62.5, launches 53.8, high passes 53.7, through balls 39.2, and crosses 30.7 percent (1826 Wyscout matches, five leagues, 2017/18).

Metrica tracking agrees with the completion-by-pass-kind figures when passes are split by length: under 10 metres 82 to 89 percent, 10 to 25 metres 92 percent, 25 to 40 metres 70 to 72 percent, and over 40 metres 58 percent (2 matches, 25 frames per second tracking plus events).
The duel is the most common contested action in football at 456 a match, 87 of them aerial, and the engine models no duel at all (1826 Wyscout matches, five leagues, 2017/18).

The ball sits above 1 metre for 12.4 percent of tracked frames in nine European top-league matches and 19.4 percent in twenty A-League matches, and above 2 metres for 7.6 and 10.6 percent, reaching 12 to 15 metres at its highest (SkillCorner tracking, A-League 2024/25).

Ball height is standard in tracking data rather than exotic: kloppy (version 3.19.0) types every tracking frame's ball position as a three-dimensional point and fills in the height for Tracab, Sportec, StatsPerform, SkillCorner, PFF, Second Spectrum, Signality, and HawkEye.

The minimum event fields that kloppy and floodlight agree on are the event type, the period and timestamp, the start coordinates and (where the event has an end) the end coordinates, the team identifier, the player identifier, and an outcome.

The ball is in play for 59 percent of recorded frames, about 55 minutes, and its speed has a median of 5.9 metres per second, a ninetieth percentile of 15.1, and a maximum near 57 (2 Metrica matches, 25 frames per second).

Most possession is brief: a match holds about 475 possession chains, 67.8 percent of them carry no pass or one pass, the median chain lasts 2.9 seconds, and only one chain in 20 ends in a shot (2 Metrica matches).

The duel is a first-class contested action with types for ground attacking, ground defending, aerial, loose ball, and tackle, resolved from both players' attributes, their mood, and the ball's height and speed. It was first framed as the single place where player quality becomes an outcome; the person later corrected that part, so the duel is one such place among many.
items.why: Asked whether the duel becomes a primitive, the person said yes, a first-class contested action; the data had shown the duel is the most common contested action and the engine modelled none.

items.text: A player on the ball has an opponent within 5 metres for 56 percent of touches, with the nearest opponent a median 4.4 metres away, and has on average only 1.16 teammates within 10 metres (3366 StatsBomb 360 freeze frames).

High intensity concentrates into attacking sequences rather than spreading across the match: during goal-scoring sequences players average 3.16 metres per second and spend 8.8 percent of the time above 7 metres per second, against a match average of 1.67 and 0.25 to 0.44 percent (19 goal sequences at 20 frames per second, Last Row data).

Across all passes, pressure appears not to matter, moving completion by only seven points and not in order, because the purpose of a pass is confounded with pressure; restricted to flat passes the curve is monotone and spans twenty points, from 79.8 percent with an opponent inside two metres to 100 percent beyond twelve (1650 passes joined to tracking within 9 milliseconds).
items.evidence: .scratch/out/idsse_sync.csv (1650 passes joined to tracking at 9 ms)

items.text: The duel is the second most common on-ball event at 201.7 a match in DFL data, which reconciles the earlier figure of 456 a match because Wyscout logs one row per participant while DFL logs one per contest; a duel turns the ball over in only 29.4 percent of cases (7 DFL matches, 9961 events).

The ground duel is sharply asymmetric: when the ball carrier wins, possession changes hands 6.4 percent of the time, and when the defender wins it changes 51.4 percent, while the aerial duel is nearly symmetric at 31.2 against 36.6 percent, so a model with one win probability and an automatic turnover would roughly double real turnover rates (7 DFL matches).

Fouls are an outcome of the duel rather than a separate mechanism: 10.6 percent of duels resolve as a foul, giving 21.4 a match against the 22.9 foul events the schema records, so an engine that models duels obtains fouls, free kicks, and cautions without a separate foul generator (7 DFL matches).

Every action family is a place where player quality becomes an outcome, and the duel is only one of them: passes, through balls, positioning, off-ball movement, dribbles, shooting, goalkeeper actions, blocking and shielding, tackles and duels, and carrying and progressing the ball each need their own resolution.
items.why: The person corrected the board for treating the duel as the single place quality shows, naming the rest of the game; the data had already shown the pass has a completion surface a duel model does not produce.

items.text: The duel looked dominant partly because the DFL schema files several action families inside one element: take-ons at 14.6 a match with 65.7 percent success, shielding as retained control at 17.6, and beaten defenders at 7.3 all live inside the TacklingGame element, so its 201.7 contests a match are a container rather than a single action (7 DFL matches).

Evidence now covers the pass, through ball, cross, shot, dribble, duel, shot block, positioning, and aggregate off-ball movement, while three families have no outcome evidence at all: the carry, which no schema read records as an event; the ten off-ball run types that SkillCorner names but nothing has counted; and shielding outside a recorded duel.

The full action set is 53 actions, 38 outfield and 15 goalkeeper; public data measures 39 in full and 10 partially, and feints only thinly, and nothing public measures marking and cover assignments, keeper organisation, or keeper dive movement.

The carry is measured on three providers: 273 to 287 carries of at least 5 metres a match (corrected from an earlier 271), at about 4 metres per second, with 79.9 percent kept, longer carries faster and riskier, and centre-backs carrying the most because they receive with the most space (7 DFL matches among the sources).

Pressure at the moment of receiving is the common input across actions: from no pressure to very high pressure, possession loss rises from 1.0 to 32.6 percent, pass completion falls from 93.4 to 67.0 percent, and one-touch play rises from 5.6 to 31.3 percent; DFL tracking gives the same gradient from geometry alone, 93.4 percent kept with no opponent inside 10 metres against 60.9 with one inside 1 metre (20 SkillCorner matches).

Off-ball runs happen 495 times a match across ten subtypes, and a run's danger and its completion move in opposite directions: safe runs such as coming short and dropping off are received 91 to 98 percent of the time when targeted and almost never lead to a shot, while runs in behind and runs to receive a cross are received 40 to 52 percent of the time and lead to a shot 20 to 29 percent of the time (20 SkillCorner matches).

A single pressing engagement is credited with a regain only 18.5 percent of the time, yet 80.6 percent of pressing chains end in a regain, and pressing in the opponent's third regains 32.6 percent against 25.4 in midfield, so the value of pressing is collective (200 StatsBomb matches).

Bodies between the ball and the goal decide shots: with no defender in the shot cone a shot scores 12.4 percent of the time and is blocked 20.9 percent, with two defenders it scores 5.4 and is blocked 40.4, and a shooter has an opponent inside 5 metres 88.2 percent of the time (4671 non-penalty shots with StatsBomb 360 frames).

A keeper's save rate falls with shot quality, from 89.1 percent below 0.05 expected goals to 27.2 percent above 0.4; two saves in three are not held (a fifth go behind and a fifth are parried into danger), and 87 percent of goals are conceded without the keeper touching the ball (200 StatsBomb matches).

Keeper depth follows a measured rule: out of possession with the ball in the keeper's own half, depth is about 0.23 metres per metre of ball distance from goal, the keeper spends 42 percent of live time beyond the depth of the box, shifts 0.17 metres sideways per metre the ball moves across, and stands a median 2.2 metres off the line at the moment of a shot, where depth has no effect on conversion once shot quality is known (7 DFL matches).

Keepers distribute 66 times a match between them at 73.5 percent completion, with short passes and throws above 97 percent and punts at 29.1; short goal kicks are 45.3 percent of goal kicks and complete at 99.4 percent against 44.1 for long ones, and the 2019 goal-kick law halved the median goal kick from 65.6 metres in 2017/18 to 31.3 metres in 2020 to 2024 (200 StatsBomb matches).

Dribbles happen 27.4 times a match at 53.0 percent success, success falls up the pitch from 61.5 percent in a team's own third to 48.2 in the final third, and role changes how often a player dribbles but not how often the dribble succeeds: wingers attempt six times as many as centre-backs, at about the same success rate as full-backs and forwards (200 StatsBomb matches).

Shielding is common but barely coded: event feeds record 1.3 shields a match, while tracking shows about 80 possessions a match held against an opponent inside 2 metres, 10 of them stationary, with about two in three kept (7 DFL matches).

The decision to shoot is a steep threshold at the edge of the box: 87.7 percent of on-ball releases inside 6 metres are shots, 72.1 at 6 to 11 metres, 35.3 at 11 to 16.5, 20.2 at 16.5 to 22, and 6.2 at 22 to 30, and pressure halves the shooting rate outside 11 metres; under pressure the share of releases that are passes falls from 85.5 to 52.9 percent as clearances, dribbles, and dispossessions appear (200 StatsBomb matches).

Players choose the safe open option more often than the dangerous one: over 70,059 passes with freeze frames, a four-term score (space around the receiver, clearance of the passing lane, distance, and forward progress) picks the real receiver 55.5 percent of the time against 14.9 by chance, and among SkillCorner's tracked options the safest is chosen 45.0 percent of the time and the most threatening 31.7, below the 36.0 chance rate (200 StatsBomb matches and 20 SkillCorner matches).

items.text: The match changes with the clock: minutes 75 to 90 produce goals 41 percent faster than minutes 0 to 15 and added time 70 percent faster, passing tempo falls from 10.3 to 8.2 passes a minute and to 7.0 in added time, and cautions rise fivefold (1826 Wyscout league matches).

The score changes behaviour once team strength is removed: a team trailing by one goal scores at 1.10 times its own expected rate and a team leading by one at 0.92; the trailing team's possession rises above its expectation from 2 points early to 12 points after the 90th minute; the leading team takes its throw-ins, goal kicks, and free kicks at a median 22.0 seconds against 15.1 for the trailing team; and the team that scores first wins 69.4 percent of the time (1826 Wyscout matches, strength-adjusted, and 7 DFL matches).

items.text: The gap an attribute makes between players lives in four places at once: in the choice a player makes (the pass picked, the moment to shoot), in the duel, in the body (pace, strength, stamina), and in the repeat, so a strong player also has fewer bad days.
items.why: Having chosen to amplify attribute effects so a management game rewards a better player, the person placed the gap in all four places.

items.text: When the realism programme changes the event contract, the contract copies a real provider schema in full rather than a core subset, so the engine's output can feed any tool that reads that schema.
items.why: The person accepted the true size of the contract change rather than a core subset, so the output could be read by existing tools for that schema.

items.text: The event contract mixes two providers: it keeps every DFL event kind and attribute and adds what StatsBomb carries that DFL does not, such as the freeze frame of player positions at each shot; this amends the earlier choice to copy a single provider schema in full.

The engine keeps one internal record of each match, with one definition per event kind, and both the test-only output and the event contract are written from that record, so they can differ in what they show but never in a fact.
items.why: The person asked for a worked example first, then chose one record with two views so the realism test can never pass a match whose reported events disagree with what it measured.

items.text: Where DFL and StatsBomb define the same event kind differently, the DFL definition wins, and StatsBomb only adds what DFL lacks.
items.why: Providers count the same action very differently, so a merged contract must pick one definition for each shared kind.

items.text: An in-match knock is handled by all three parties according to severity: the medical staff take a severe injury off at once; for a minor knock the player's personality decides whether to play on, and the manager sees the knock and can overrule at the next stoppage; playing on raises the chance the knock becomes an injury and lowers the player's output.
items.why: It answers the long-open question of whether a manager may keep a hurt player on the pitch, and the person confirmed this severity split as their reading.

items.text: A severe injury is carried across seasons more gently than in real football: a long absence, a shorter dip in form, and no career ended by injury, with personality and the medical staff moving a single player's return around that average.

On the ground, local numbers decide duels: with all 1,412 DFL duels joined to tracking, the defender wins 42.7 percent when outnumbered within 5 metres, 44.2 when level, 53.2 with one extra teammate, and 66.7 with two, while in the air support makes no difference once the defender is not outnumbered (7 DFL matches, tracking joined to events).
items.evidence: .scratch/out/gap_idsse_an.txt (7 DFL matches, tracking joined to events) and FINDINGS.md §16

items.text: Loose balls are a real phase: a clearance is next controlled by the clearing team only 26.5 percent of the time, the team of a player who wins a header controls the next ball only 48.0 percent of the time against 39.3 for the loser's team, and 6.2 percent of shots are rebounds within 5 seconds, which convert at 16.4 percent against 11.3 (200 StatsBomb matches).

The ball is dead for 42.2 minutes a match, and each restart has a measured stoppage: a throw-in takes a median 13.8 seconds, a goal kick 23.2, a corner 31.8, a free kick 32.5, and the kick-off after a goal 68.2 (7 DFL matches, tracking joined to events).
items.evidence: .scratch/out/gap_idsse_an.txt (7 DFL matches, tracking joined to events) and FINDINGS.md §16

items.text: Full match simulation covers every match in the leagues the player chose; the simulated past and every other league keep the fast result-only model used at save creation and for unchosen leagues, so the rule that every other match is a full simulation amends neither.
items.why: Running every match everywhere as a full simulation would cost minutes per season before any realism addition, so the person limited it to the active leagues.

items.text: The referee's home leaning, the rate of injuries during a match, and the effect of weather and pitch wear are all sized from published data rather than set by design, so the seventh build step needs a research pass before its design targets exist.
items.why: The person chose data over design where data is missing.

items.text: The game has a video assistant referee: some goals, penalties, and red cards are checked and overturned, with the delays real football has, and whether a competition uses it can depend on the competition.

The event contract uses the game's own names and structure from the start, with a mapping to the DFL and StatsBomb schemas, so no licence can block it. This amends the earlier choices to copy a provider schema and to merge DFL with StatsBomb, so no outside tool reads the output directly, while the rule that DFL wins each definition conflict still decides each definition.
items.why: Writing the contract in the game's own words removes the licence risk.

items.text: Referees favour the home side measurably: in Serie A 2007-08 matches played behind closed doors, home bias was estimated at 23 percent for fouls, 26 percent for yellow cards, and 70 percent for red cards; Champions League referees gave away teams 25 percent more yellow cards than home teams and Europa League referees 10 percent more, after controlling for dominance.

The crowd drives the referee's leaning: in Bundesliga matches without spectators during COVID-19, the home team's foul advantage of about 0.6 a match reversed to about one foul against, home cards rose significantly, the bias scales with crowd size, and home advantage in results shrank but did not vanish.

Added time leans towards the home side: referees add about 44 seconds less when the home team leads by one goal than when the away team does, about 60 seconds less than an unbiased benchmark with fans present, and the gap disappears without a crowd (from a study summary only).

A video assistant referee overturns a decision about once every three to four matches: 109 overturns in the 2019-20 Premier League season from about 2,400 checks, and 123 in 2020-21, split into 34 goals awarded, 42 disallowed, 29 penalties awarded, and 22 penalties overturned, with an average delay of about 50 seconds per review; LaLiga reviews about 12.55 incidents a match.

Elite match injury incidence is about 21 injuries per 1000 match hours in 2022-23, down from 27.5 in 2001 to 2008, which is roughly one match injury per team every two to three matches; hamstring injuries are 24 percent of all injuries and rising.

Injury risk rises late in each half, with fixture congestion (5 of 8 studies find more match injuries with 4 days or fewer of rest, and muscle injuries rise within 5 days of the previous match), and with age, at an odds ratio of about 1.1 a year and 1.4 a year for hamstring strains.

Conditions are measured only in part: altitude moves the expected goal difference by about half a goal per 1000 metres of difference, heat cuts running distance sharply (about 26 percent at 43 degrees against 21 degrees, weakly sourced), artificial turf shifts the injury mix toward ankle sprains (4.83 against 2.66 per 1000 match hours) without raising elite injury totals, and no source quantifies rain, wind, or pitch wear.

A referee who leans towards the home side reads as realism rather than as the game cheating the player. Published research now measures that leaning (in fouls, cards, and added time) and ties it to the crowd, so the game copies a real effect rather than inventing one.

Flight arcs, heading duels, and spin on every ball update fit inside the 10 percent CPU tripwire the engine build records. Tracking data puts the ball above 1 metre for 12 to 19 percent of frames, so the aerial path is not a rare branch.
Whether a manager may keep a hurt player on the pitch is still unanswered; giving injuries a severity and a risk driven by play settles severity and risk, but not the manager's choice.
A realism budget measured against the shipped engine can be chosen before the additions are built, and the engine stays fast enough to run 1000 calibration matches inside it.
The engine can model the duel as a first-class contested action at roughly 456 a match without breaching its performance budget.

Each action family gets its own resolution model, with the action kind and the situation as the first inputs and the player's attributes and mood as the second, so no single family carries player quality for the rest.

A hand-built choice model (the release mix by zone and pressure, a shooting threshold by distance, and a four-term receiver score with a pressure modifier) reproduces the measured shooting threshold at the edge of the box and the preference for the safe open receiver closely enough, without a learned model.

Making pitch wear and weather interact pulled against the planned realism test of three aggregate bands held over 1000 matches: either the bands must hold across every combination of conditions, or calibration fixes the conditions and so never tests them. Resolved: calibration groups runs by condition band (dry, wet, worn) and sets a band for each, so a condition is expected to move the numbers rather than fail the test.

Real per-match rates vary by only about one percentage point in pass accuracy and two shots in shot volume across five leagues, while the planned bands were goals 2.4 to 3.2, shots 8 to 16 per team, and possession 35 to 65 percent, several times wider than the real spread, so the test as planned would pass an engine that is visibly wrong. Resolved: four measured families (per-match rates, the scoreline distribution and home advantage, pass completion as a curve by kind and length, and physical output) replace the three bands, and the assumption that the three bands would still hold is rejected with them.

Banding physical output and making the duel the place where player quality becomes an outcome both need the engine to report per-player data, but the event contract carries no player identifier, and the event-contract change (already repriced as a full redesign) is deferred to the realism programme, so the chosen test could not run against the engine the board had agreed to ship. Resolved: the test reads a separate test-only output with per-player data, so it runs against the shipped engine and the deferral holds.

The findings that pressure matters only once pass purpose is separated, and that flat-pass completion is set by pitch position rather than by person, argued with how the board had framed player quality: completion is set by the kind of action and the situation first and the player second, so a uniform per-player attribute gives the wrong answer by role even with the right values. The duel already bet on emergence, nothing said the same for the pass, and the planned realism test could not tell the two models apart. Measurement then put the situational spread of pass completion at 18.3 points against a player spread of 3.6, with the same pattern for shooting and saving while duels are player-heavy, so the test can tell the models apart by banding the per-player residual spread. Resolved in favour of situation first and player second for the pass, the shot, and the save, with the duel keeping a larger player share.

The duel had been made the single place where player quality becomes an outcome, while the person's correction says every action family is such a place, and the pass data already showed a completion surface a duel model does not produce. Resolved in favour of every action family: the duel stays a first-class contested action but loses the word single, and the bet that a duel model would reproduce the pass completion curve as an emergent result is rejected.

The realism test reads a separate test-only output while the game reads the event contract, and the contract then became a full provider schema; two outputs report the same match, the test checks one and the player sees the other, so the test could pass a match whose reported events disagree with what it measured. Resolved: both outputs are written from one internal record with one definition per event kind.

Merging DFL and StatsBomb into one contract pulled against the measured fact that providers count the same action very differently: where both schemas define the same event kind, the merged contract must pick one definition, and the promised benefit of output that any tool for that schema can read holds for neither provider in full. Resolved: DFL wins every conflict, so each shared kind has one definition.

Making DFL the definition of every shared event kind pulled against banding most on-ball and keeper families against StatsBomb over 200 matches, because the public DFL set is only 7 matches, too few to band most families on its own definitions; either the StatsBomb-measured bands are converted to DFL definitions, or the bands are measured on 7 matches. Resolved: the StatsBomb bands are converted and the 7 DFL matches check each conversion, with the assumption that every StatsBomb definition has a close enough DFL equivalent carrying the risk.

Simulating several past seasons in full at save creation pulled against the engine's cost: one league season takes about 20 seconds on eight cores with today's engine, so five seasons across five leagues is about eight minutes before the realism additions make each match more expensive; either save creation becomes a long wait, or the past seasons run a cheaper match than the one the player sees. Resolved: the past runs on a fast result-only model, with the assumption that it can be calibrated to the full engine carrying the risk.

The career test bands injury after-effects against real data (two seasons below par, and 20 percent of professional careers ended within three seasons after an ACL rupture), while the choice to carry severe injuries more gently makes the dip shorter and ends no career; the injury band would therefore fail by design, as the amplified per-player band does, unless it is dropped or re-sized. Resolved: the injury band is re-sized to a softer target set on purpose.

Keeping every match other than the player's own as a full simulation, with realism before speed, pulled against running the simulated past and every unchosen league on a fast result-only model; either those matches become full simulations, which the engine's measured cost prices at minutes per season before any realism addition, or full simulation covers only the active leagues. Resolved: full simulation is limited to the active leagues.
A season layer comes into scope: fixtures, results, and form are modelled properly, so this board describes a product larger than the match engine.
items.why: Form and season context cannot be supplied as asserted numbers in a team file; they need a season model behind them, so they are earned rather than asserted.

items.text: The season layer contains fixtures and results, form, a league table with standings, season-long squad availability with suspensions, injury persistence, and carried fitness, and a full club calendar with cups, fixture congestion, and rotation.
Form is computed at two scopes, a team form and a per-player form, and the per-player form feeds the player's mood, the mood that the match itself moves and that drives the player's decisions.
A new save generates a synthetic backstory of past seasons, so partnerships, form, and club reputation start at believable values in the first match.
items.why: Partnerships between players cannot be generated for a squad without a shared history to derive them from, so the season layer supplies that history.

items.text: The club calendar and season-long squad availability are one piece, because fixture congestion and rotation matter only when fitness and suspensions carry between matches.

The board believed the match event carried only a team identifier, a score, and four event types (kick-off, goal, full-time, and tactics-change) and no player identifier. The code by the fifth session shows 17 event types and an optional player identifier, in the protocol crate's event definition.
items.evidence: crates/protocol/src/event.rs:16 and crates/protocol/src/event.rs:146 (17 event types and an optional player identifier, at session 5)

items.text: The event contract gains its player identifier when the work to build the season layer starts and not before; the engine ships on the contract it has, and the realism programme pays the migration across every part of the build that reads the event stream by then.
items.why: The stream-protocol part of the engine build was already complete with other parts depending on it, and changing the contract later was judged cheaper than disturbing a complete piece of work now.

items.text: The generated backstory is one past season deep: a form record, a final table position, and partnerships earned from minutes played together. This was later replaced by several fully simulated past seasons.
The season layer includes transfers and finances, with a market, budgets, and wages, so the product is a full football-management game rather than a match engine with a season around it.

A player's ability changes over seasons along age curves, one per attribute, and the curves differ from player to player with the variance real players show in how they develop. Many other factors move the curves, and which factors they are is still open.
The manager runs a training plan between matches, setting focus and intensity, and training moves fitness, injury risk, the squad's familiarity with each tactic, and player development.
Five factors move a player's age curves: playing time and the level played at, training and coaching, injuries, personality, and moments. The list stays open, so other factors may be added later.

Moments are of two kinds and both move a player's curve: match moments such as a debut, a decisive goal, or a costly error in a final, and career turning points such as a transfer, a loan, a new manager, or a first-team breakthrough.

A new save simulates several past seasons in full at save creation, so every player's current ability, partnerships, and reputation agree with a simulated past. This replaces the earlier plan of a backstory only one past season deep.
items.why: One past season was judged not enough history for a partnership to read as earned.

items.text: Today's engine plays one match in 387 milliseconds of wall time on one core of an AMD Ryzen 7 9800X3D, so one 20-club league season of 380 matches takes about 147 seconds on one core and about 20 seconds on eight, before any realism addition makes a match more expensive. The match time is measured by the engine benchmark; the season figures are arithmetic.
The past seasons simulated at save creation run a fast result-only model instead of the full match, so save creation stays short while the present runs the full engine.
items.why: Running every past match on the full engine would make save creation too slow; a single league season already takes minutes on one core.

items.text: The largest public career dataset is derived from Transfermarkt: 50,000 players, 65 competitions, 1.89 million appearances with minutes, 650,000 market valuations, and 175,000 transfers, released under CC0. It measures playing time, level, moves, and market judgement, and it carries no ratings.

Performance peaks at about 27.4 across 15,591 top-five-league player-seasons, at 26 to 27 for wingers and full-backs and at 27.5 to 28 for centre-backs and strikers. Wingers fall to half their peak by 31 and centre-backs by 35.2, and an 18-year-old in a top league plays at 50 to 85 percent of the eventual peak.

Physical output has its own curves: across 5,203 GPS match performances speed peaks at 25.7, endurance at 24.8, and explosiveness at 26.0, and high-intensity output falls after 32 while endurance holds. Creative passing holds into the early thirties while shooting and tackling fade.

Of about 200 LaLiga academy players aged 13 to 18, 4 percent reached the top tier within ten years. Across 378 Bundesliga loans, loanees gained no measurable minutes and no measurable market value compared with 6,162 players who were not loaned.

After an ACL rupture 80 percent of elite players return, after a mean of 216 days; they stay below matched controls for two seasons, with attackers declining further, 20 percent of professionals see their careers end within three seasons, and only 47.5 percent keep their playing level.

No public data records true attribute histories, training or coaching effects at scale, personality across a career, or the causal effect of a moment. The only attribute-style history is the FIFA 15 to 23 rating set, which is rated by people rather than measured.
A loan's effect varies widely with the club, the coach, and the minutes, and it can help or hurt, while the average effect across loans stays near zero, as the Bundesliga loan study measures.
items.why: It keeps the only measured evidence on loans true while still letting a single loan matter to a player's career.

items.text: Each club has a board and an owner type, for example patient, ambitious, or frugal, that sets targets for league position, cups, finances, and style, sets how much patience the board has, and can sack the manager; sackings apply to AI managers as well.

A transfer fee is a shared market valuation plus a premium from each club's own view, and the season test bands the resulting fees against real fees and valuations by age and position from the public Transfermarkt career dataset.
The shared market valuation comes only from what every club can see (age, minutes, level, goals, recent fees, and reputation), as a Transfermarkt value does, and it never reads the true attributes.
items.why: A valuation computed from the true attributes would tell every club the truth that scouting noise hides, and clubs would stop disagreeing about a player.

items.text: A sacked human manager keeps the save: the manager is unemployed, can apply for jobs, and receives offers based on reputation.
The player chooses at save creation which countries and divisions are active, so more leagues give more jobs and more clubs to deal with, at the cost of a slower season.

A club has four income sources: matchday income from stadium size, prices, and attendance; broadcast and prize money by league position and cup progress; commercial income from reputation and success; and owner money that the club's owner type can put in or take out within limits.

Every league the player did not choose runs the fast result-only model used for the simulated past, so its players play, develop, and gain value, and the whole world moves while only the chosen leagues run the full engine.

The revenue mix is measured: the top 20 clubs earn 43 percent from commercial income, 38 percent from broadcast, and 19 percent from matchday. The top ten lean on commercial income at 48 percent while clubs ranked 11 to 20 lean on broadcast at 49 percent, and the Premier League as a whole takes about half of its 6.8 billion pounds from broadcast (Deloitte Football Money League and Annual Review).
items.evidence: https://www.deloitte.com/uk/en/services/consulting-financial/analysis/deloitte-football-money-league.html and the Deloitte Annual Review pages (research sub-agent, batch 49)

items.text: In a selling league player sales are a main income source: across nine Eredivisie clubs in 2022/23 they were 29.5 percent of income on average and about 44 percent at Ajax and PSV.

Revenue spread inside a league is set largely by broadcast rules: Premier League central payments run 1.6 to 1 from bottom to top with about 2.7 million pounds of merit pay per place, Bundesliga TV money runs 2.7 to 1, two clubs take 52 percent of LaLiga revenue, and Eredivisie revenue runs about 10 to 1.

Wages run at 54 to 80 percent of revenue across the big-five leagues (Bundesliga 54, LaLiga 60, Premier League 65, Serie A 66, Ligue 1 80), and UEFA's squad-cost rule caps wages, transfer costs, and agent fees at 70 percent of revenue from 2025/26.
items.evidence: the Deloitte Annual Review pages and https://www.uefa.com/news-media/news/0274-14da0ce4535d-fa5b130ae9b6-1000--explainer-uefa-s-new-financial-sustainability-regulations/ (research sub-agent, batch 49)

items.text: Losses are normal and owners cover them: European top-division clubs lost 1.1 billion euros before tax in 2024, only 8 Premier League clubs made an operating profit, and Championship clubs lost 355 million pounds with one club in operating profit. Owner-funding totals are only a proxy built from club examples.

The richest league buys and the others sell: in summer 2025 Premier League clubs spent 3.0 billion pounds gross, about 44 percent of league revenue and 51 percent of all big-five gross spending, while the Bundesliga and Ligue 1 were net sellers by 180 and 305 million euros.

Prize money is published in full: the Champions League pays 18.62 million euros for the league phase, 2.1 million per win, and rising round payments up to 18.5 million for the final, from a 2.467 billion euro pot, against 565 million for the Europa League.
Player-sale income enters the club's finances, and the club's owner type decides how much of it reaches the manager's budgets and how much pays debts or wages.
items.why: Real selling clubs earn a large share of their income from player sales, and with only four income sources a selling club in the game could not earn what a real one does.

items.text: Leagues and competitions carry financial rules such as a squad-cost cap, and a breach brings a sanction: a fine, a transfer ban, or a points deduction.

The work to build the season layer splits into four cards: competitions (table, cups, calendar, congestion, suspensions), squad and careers (form, availability, training, development, the simulated past), the market (scouting, valuation, fees, transfers, loans), and club business (board and owner, income, wages, financial rules, sacking, the job market).
items.why: The season layer had grown too large for one piece of work, and smaller cards can each start on their own.

items.text: A later version of the game loads a real-life database whose players start at the current real season, possibly imported by the player, so the world must accept imported seasons; until then the player chooses how many past seasons a new save simulates.

Leagues, cups, and competitions mirror the real European structure in full, starting with the leagues of every UEFA member association, with their divisions, promotion and relegation, domestic cups, and European qualification.
AI clubs get the effect of training from their staff quality and their manager, with no day-by-day plan; only the player's club runs the detailed training plan the manager sets between matches.
Manager sacking rates and board patience are sized from published data rather than set by design.
items.why: The person asked for it to be looked up, and then for every open data gap to be researched before the board continued.

items.text: Managers are sacked often and sacking does not work: the median top-flight tenure is about 243 days, 47 English managers were dismissed in 2014-15 and 51 in 2025-26, and across 331 mid-season changes in the top two divisions of five countries from 2017-18 to 2021-22, points collapsed before a dismissal while expected points stayed stable, and the new manager's effect against matched controls was indistinguishable from zero.

A sacking follows results against expectation rather than underlying performance: a run of defeats, the relegation zone, and results worse than the pre-season bookmaker expectation all raise the risk, and of 78 Premier League clubs that sacked a manager in the relegation zone, 58 percent went down anyway. No study compares sacking rates by owner type or measures how fast a sacked manager finds work.

The CIES transfer-value model estimates fees from performance, age, position, contract length, and club, and its estimates correlate with fees paid at 76 to 86 percent. In 34 of 49 cases studied the fee sat within 2 million euros of the estimate, with a long tail of star overpayment such as Mbappe at 87 million euros over.

UEFA has 55 member associations, 53 of which place clubs in European competition, with places set by a five-year coefficient. The three club competitions use a 36-club league phase since 2024-25, and the official 2025-26 access list defines which domestic place enters which round.

League formats vary by country beyond a double round robin: championship and relegation splits (Belgium, Scotland, Austria), relegation play-offs (Germany, France), promotion play-offs (England, Spain), spring-to-autumn calendars in the Nordic leagues, different winter breaks, cups with or without extra time and two-legged ties, and a FIFA calendar that merges the September and October international windows from 2026.

Historical league and cup results exist as public-domain JSON in openfootball on GitHub, as free CSV with unclear commercial terms at football-data.co.uk, and as CC BY-SA tables on Wikipedia; RSSSF is the deepest archive and offers no bulk export.

Real names reach football games through collective licences (FIFPRO for player image rights, plus league and club licences) or through community real-names files that the player imports into a game that ships fictional names. The import pattern has run for over a decade without a reported successful lawsuit, but no court has tested it, and a broken rights chain cost EA about 100 million dollars with Brazilian players.

The match engine ships first and the season layer builds on it, so no season requirement changes the engine's data contract after the fact. Rejected, because the decision to add the player identifier to the event contract when the season layer starts changes that contract after the fact on purpose.
A generated backstory produces a history that holds together: a club's past results, its partnerships, and its reputation agree with each other and with the squad on the books.
Per-player match ratings can be derived from the event stream the engine already emits. Rejected by a read of the code at the time, which found no player identifier on the match event.

The realism programme still fits the earlier decision that every idea on this board belongs to one second workflow, separate from the match-engine build, although the full season layer (table, availability, calendar, and cups) makes that workflow larger than the match engine it follows. Rejected when the work was split into two programmes, engine realism and the season layer.

The cost of changing the event contract after the viewer, commentary, and report parts of the engine build are built is acceptable, and it is smaller than the cost of disturbing a complete part of the build today; every consumer of the event stream being still unbuilt today is the reason to doubt it.

One past season is enough history for a partnership to read as earned, so a pair with one season of shared minutes is distinguishable from a pair with none. Rejected when the save moved to several simulated past seasons.

A transfer market and finances can be built on the attributes that the work to deepen the player model supplies, with no scouting model, no contract-negotiation model, and no separate player-value model.
Public data on real careers is enough to size age curves per attribute and the player-to-player variance around them, even though real data measures performance rather than attributes.

A real age curve measured on performance converts to an attribute curve through the same deliberate amplification the game applies to attribute effects (made larger than their measured sizes so that a management game rewards a better player), so a player's decline reads on the pitch at the size real careers show.
Moments are one source of the player-to-player variance that real career data measures around the age curves, not an extra spread on top of it, so the curves as a whole still match real careers.

A result-only model can be calibrated to the full engine's results (scorelines, player totals, injuries, and development inputs such as minutes and moments) closely enough that a simulated past reads as the same football as the present.

Training, coaching, and personality effects on development are set by design rather than by data, because no public data sizes them, and the career test bands only the factors the public research measures: playing time and level from the Transfermarkt career data, age peaks, physical curves, academy and loan outcomes, and ACL recovery.
The spread of loan outcomes can be set by design, because the Bundesliga loan study measures only the average effect of a loan and not the spread around it.
A valuation built from visible data only can be banded directly against the 650,000 Transfermarkt valuations in the public career dataset, because both read the same kind of visible inputs.

Owner types and financial rules together reproduce the measured shape of club losses (most clubs losing money and owners covering it within the rules) without a band that forces the share of loss-making clubs.
Real player and club names, likenesses, and badges can reach the game through a database the player imports, so the game itself ships no data that needs a licence.
The result-only model can run the leagues of all 55 UEFA member associations at once without making each matchday wait, because only the leagues the player chose run the full engine.

Making a loan a career turning point that moves a player's curve pulled against the study of 378 Bundesliga loans, which found loanees gained no measurable minutes and no measurable market value; a game in which a loan develops a player departs from the only measured evidence on loans. Resolved when the person chose to let a loan help or hurt with an average effect near zero, which keeps the study true, with the spread of outcomes set by design.

Giving a club four income sources pulled against the measurements that player sales are a main source of income in every league but the richest, at 29.5 percent of income in the Eredivisie; a selling club in the game could not earn what a real selling club earns unless transfer income became a fifth source. Resolved when player-sale income was brought into the club's finances, with the owner type deciding where it goes.

The board believed the attribute schema held 37 attributes in four groups, with no personality attribute, no hidden trait, and no positional-familiarity value. The schema file shows 36 attributes, nine per group, when it was read again in session 5.
items.evidence: content/attributes.json:1 (36 attributes, nine per group, at session 5)

items.text: Where an attribute and a personality trait overlap, they split by scope: the attribute acts on each action in a match (composure on a shot under pressure, aggression on a tackle), and the trait acts on occasions and choices (a final, a penalty shoot-out, whether to dive or to foul cynically).
items.why: Otherwise the engine would read two values for one behaviour without saying what each one moves that the other does not.

items.text: Four more traits join the eight already chosen, for twelve in all: versatility (willingness to play out of position), controversy (trouble off the pitch), money motivation (how much wages decide moves), and bravery (readiness for a 50-50, a header in traffic, or a block).

The player record gains a fifth attribute group, personality, with its own slots outside the 50-attribute limit, so the twelve traits stop competing with new performance attributes for the 13 free slots. The record changes when the realism programme starts, as the decision on when the player record changes shape allows.
items.why: The twelve traits alone would take 12 of the 13 free slots and leave one slot for every new performance attribute.

items.text: A player record carries an identifier, a name, a shirt number, one position code, and attributes. It carries no age, no preferred foot, no height, and no starting condition.
A player has exactly one position code, drawn from ten: GK, CB, LB, RB, DM, CM, AM, LW, RW, ST.
All four absent player fields matter: personality and traits; condition, morale, and form; age, height, and preferred foot; and positional familiarity.
A player carries a competence rating for every position the player can fill, not one position code, so picking a lineup is a trade-off rather than slot-filling.
items.why: Picking a lineup should be a trade-off between players rather than filling slots.

items.text: The gap between a strong player and a weak one is three things together: fewer errors, a higher ceiling of attempted actions, and more consistency.
items.why: Any one of the three on its own would read as a flat multiplier.

items.text: New performance-related and personality-related attributes should be created beyond the 37 the schema was believed to carry at the time.
A player carries a mood that the match itself moves, and that mood drives the player's decisions.
Personality decides how strongly the player's own mood and the team's mood change that player's decisions; personality is the mediator, not a third mood.

The board believed the attribute schema accepts 30 to 50 attributes in four fixed groups with 13 free slots, so any personality attribute would have to be declared in an existing group such as mental. The schema file holds 36 attributes, so 14 slots are free, as read in session 5.
items.evidence: content/attributes.json:1 (36 attributes, so 14 slots are free, at session 5)

items.text: Clubs disagree about a player's worth for two reasons at once: each club sees a noisy estimate of the attributes, set by its scouting quality, and each club weighs the attributes differently by its playing identity and its manager's attributes.
items.why: If every club saw every attribute exactly, no club could value a player differently from another, and the market would have no disagreement to trade on.

items.text: The player record changes shape when the realism programme starts and not before, following the precedent set for the event contract, which gains its player identifier only when the season-layer work starts. The match-rules and tactics-and-ai slices are therefore built against a record that will change under them.
items.why: It follows the same timing already chosen for the event contract change.

items.text: An outfield player covers 9.6 to 10.3 kilometres per match, spends about 70 percent of the time below 2 metres per second, and sprints above 7 metres per second for 0.25 to 0.44 percent of the match, covering 100 to 200 metres at that speed. Measured from two Metrica matches of 25-frames-per-second tracking plus events.

Peak sprint velocity has a narrow spread across a league: the tenth percentile is 26.6 kilometres per hour, the median 28.3, the ninetieth percentile 29.9, and the fastest player 31.8. Measured from 20 A-League matches of 2024/25 SkillCorner tracking.

Players cover more high-speed distance out of possession than in it, 1052 against 805 metres per 90 minutes for high-speed running and 261 against 212 metres for sprinting, so defending costs more at high intensity than attacking. Measured from 20 A-League matches of 2024/25 SkillCorner tracking.

Every outfield role covers 26 to 43 metres of the pitch's length between its tenth and ninetieth percentile. Attacking midfielders roam widest laterally at 42.9 metres while full-backs stay narrowest at about 30, and central midfielders sit nearest the ball at 18.7 to 19.6 metres and within 20 metres of it for 56 to 58 percent of the match. Measured from 20 SkillCorner matches, 3.87 million player samples.

Players move about twice as fast within 5 metres of the ball as beyond 40 metres, and attackers show the steepest gradient: a striker runs 3.62 metres per second near the ball and 1.81 far from it, against a centre-back's 2.86 and 1.87. Measured from two Metrica matches at 25 frames per second.

An outfielder covers 10.25 kilometres per ninety minutes on official Bundesliga tracking, and the difference between roles lives in intensity rather than volume: a centre-back covers 84 percent of a wing-back's total distance but only 46 percent of the wing-back's high-intensity distance, 276 metres against 595 per half. Measured from 7 DFL matches, 247 full player-halves at 25 frames per second.

items.text: A player sprints above 7 metres per second for 0.7 percent of live time and runs below 2 metres per second for 45 percent of it, and no more than about one outfielder in twenty exceeds 5.5 metres per second at any instant, so top speed is an attribute the match almost never uses. Measured from 7 DFL matches, 247 full player-halves at 25 frames per second.
items.evidence: .scratch/out/idsse_players.csv (7 DFL matches, 247 full player-halves at 25 fps)

items.text: Every outfield role runs faster without the ball than with it, 2.49 metres per second against 2.20 for centre-backs and 2.86 against 2.59 for defensive midfielders, so defending costs more running than attacking and costs the deepest roles the most. Measured from 7 DFL matches, 247 full player-halves at 25 frames per second.
