items.text: Pass completion is a property of pitch position rather than of the person: among comparable players in one pair of matches, flat-pass completion runs from 98.6 percent for goalkeepers and 95 for centre-backs down to 73.2 for centre-forwards, so a uniform passing attribute would make defenders too error-prone and forwards too accurate. Measured from 1650 DFL passes joined to tracking at 9 milliseconds.
items.evidence: .scratch/out/idsse_sync.csv (1650 passes joined to tracking at 9 ms)

items.text: The late-match fall in running is dead time rather than tired legs. From minutes 0 to 30 to minutes 60 to 90, distance per minute falls 17 percent and high-speed running per minute 26 percent, but the ball is in play 27 percent less, and high-speed running per minute of live play does not fall at all; forwards are the one exception, at minus 12 percent. Measured from 7 DFL matches with tracking joined to events, recorded in the findings document.
items.evidence: .scratch/out/gap_idsse_an.txt (7 DFL matches, tracking joined to events) and FINDINGS.md §16

items.text: Attribute effects are amplified on purpose beyond the sizes measured in real football, where skill moves pass, shot, and save outcomes only a few points, because a management game must reward a better player. The per-player residual band, which the realism test gained once it could separate the situation from the player, is expected to fail by design.
items.why: A management game must reward a better player, and an engine faithful to the measured sizes may make attributes feel as though they do not matter.

items.text: A manager must see that a better player is better over a run of about five matches, through form and match ratings, rather than inside one match or only over a whole season.
Consistency narrows the spread of every action, finishing and saving included, but by a different degree for each action.
items.why: Real finishing and saving barely repeat within a season, so a graded effect makes the departure from real data deliberate rather than accidental.

items.text: Personality is hidden: the manager sees a description such as professional or volatile, whose accuracy is set by scouting quality and by time at the club, in the same way each club sees only a noisy scouting estimate of a player's attributes.
A player carries at least four personality traits (professionalism, temperament, ambition and loyalty, and leadership), and more traits are wanted beyond these four.

A player carries at least eight personality traits (professionalism, temperament, ambition and loyalty, leadership, determination, adaptability, sportsmanship, and pressure handling), each a hidden value from 1 to 100, and still more traits are wanted.
The attribute schema already carries composure, aggression, work rate, teamwork, and injury resistance in its mental and physical groups.

Skill is small beside the situation for passing, shooting, and saving, and large for duels. After the situation and binomial noise are removed, players spread by 3.6 points of pass completion against an 18.3-point situational spread, and by 2.5 points of shot conversion and 2.4 of save rate with split-half correlations of only 0.17 and 0.14; but they spread by 10.0 points in aerial duels against a 5.8-point situational spread, and by 7.6 in attacking ground duels. Measured from 1826 Wyscout league matches, recorded in the findings document.
Each foot carries its own rating, the strong foot is always 100, and two-footedness matters in play but must never become the dominant quality.

The new performance attributes are marking, off-ball movement, set-piece skills (corners, free kicks, penalties, and long throws), flair, and consistency (the attribute that narrows the spread of every action by a different degree), which with 36 attributes today stays under the 50-attribute limit. Big-match nerve is left to the pressure-handling trait.

Four limits keep two-footedness from dominating: a good weaker foot is rare and costs more in the market; the weaker foot costs something only when the ball is on that side or there is no time to shift it; the gap between the feet grows with pressure and distance; and defenders and AI managers show a one-footed player onto the weaker foot.
A player's rating for a position rises with minutes played there and with training for it over months, so a manager can retrain a player for a new position.
A player carries a few habits of play, such as cutting inside or shooting from distance, separate from attributes and personality, and training and coaching can add or remove a habit.

Under pressure or low mood a strong habit can override the manager's instruction, and the manager can see why it happened. This amends the rule that an instruction is always carried out as given: it is carried out as given unless a strong habit overrides it at such a moment.
items.why: If a habit always yielded, habits would vanish under any instruction; if it always won, the manager's instruction would be weakened.

items.text: A better player shows in four places: match ratings, statistics, visibly better choices and touches on the pitch, and staff reports whose accuracy depends on the staff's own quality.

About 21 to 27 percent of elite players are left-footed, and players use the dominant foot for about 80 percent of actions. Professionals show no significant success gap between their feet where amateurs do, and two-footed players earned a wage premium of about 20 percent with full controls. No real-data share of two-footed players exists; EA's ratings put about 1.3 to 1.8 percent of its database at the top weak-foot level. Sources: a London School of Economics Centre for Economic Performance paper and a Psychology Today article, found by a research sub-agent.
The team generator can produce believable competence ratings for every position without a scouting or history model behind them.
Personality fits the existing 1-to-100 attribute scale and needs no new data type.

The two sources of disagreement about a player's value, scouting noise and each club's own weighting, can be calibrated together, so the spread of transfer fees bands cleanly even though one valuation can be wrong for two reasons at once.
Building the match-rules and tactics-and-ai slices against a player record that will change under them costs less than delaying both slices to change the record first.

A duel resolved from attributes, mood, and ball state reproduces the real pass-completion curve by kind of pass (from 91.7 percent for a simple pass down to 30.7 percent for a cross) as an emergent result, so no probability table for each kind of pass is written by hand.

Attribute effects sized to the spreads measured in real football, about plus or minus 7 points of pass completion and 5 of shot conversion between the best and worst players, still read to a manager as real differences between players.
Consistency can be an attribute that narrows a player's match-to-match spread without adding team-level variance, so a player repeats while the team's goal distribution stays Poisson.

The degree by which consistency narrows each action follows the order in which real players repeat (duels and physical output most, passing next, finishing and saving least), so the departure from the measured skill sizes is largest where the real data repeats most.
A weaker-foot rating can give two-footed players a visible edge while real rarity and a small effect size keep two-footedness from dominating squad choices.

Competence per position, new attributes, player mood, team mood, partnerships, cohesion, two tactical phases, set-piece routines, triggers, a full referee, interacting conditions, and ball spin all enlarge the cost of each engine tick, while the tactics-and-ai slice carries a benchmark tripwire that fails it at 10 percent more CPU time or 25 percent more memory than the match-rules baseline. Resolved: the tripwire guards only the engine build, and the realism programme measures against the shipped engine with a budget of its own; the assumption that such a budget can be chosen in advance and still run 1000 calibration matches carries the cost.

Making weak players swing more and letting mood move decisions both widen match-to-match variance, while the board assumed the three calibration bands (goals, shots, possession) would survive that, and already doubted that three aggregate bands measure realism at all. Resolved: the realism test now bands the spread as well as the average (goalless matches, five-one results, and how far a team's worst match sits from its best), so it measures what those two mechanisms actually add; this rests on the assumption that real football publishes such a distribution to band against.

A transfer market with finances needs a player value and a scouting judgment, but the plan to deepen the player model into a person showed a manager every attribute in full; when every club sees every attribute exactly, no club can value a player differently from another, so the market has nothing to trade on. This was the reason to doubt the assumption that a market needs no scouting model. Resolved: clubs now see a noisy scouting estimate and weigh attributes by their own identity, the no-scouting assumption is rejected, and the assumption that the two sources of disagreement can be calibrated together carries the cost.

Making weak players swing more and letting mood move decisions both widen match-to-match variance, but real football's total-goal distribution is Poisson with a variance-to-mean ratio of 1.035, so the real variance is already fully explained by the scoring rate. Extra variance would move the engine away from real football unless the mechanisms shift the rate rather than the spread. Resolved: mood, personality, and quality now move the team's scoring rate and never the spread, so goals stay Poisson; the assumption that the engine can do this carries the cost.

Two measurements of how far each line advances when a team wins the ball disagree: SkillCorner gives the back line 3.5 metres of advance and the wide roles 9 to 12, while the DFL multi-camera feed gives the back line minus 1.4 metres and the wide roles 5.4 to 7.4. The likely cause is the possession label, because SkillCorner marks controlled phases while the DFL feed marks ball ownership on every frame, contested ones included. Resolved in favour of the DFL figures, which are ground truth and labelled by the provider; the SkillCorner figures are kept for their ordering only.

The person set the strong-versus-weak gap as errors, ceiling, and consistency together, and the plan for the player model builds attributes a manager is meant to feel. Real data shows that once the situation is removed a player moves pass completion by only about 3.6 points, shot conversion by 2.5, and save rate by 2.4, and that finishing and saving barely repeat within a season. An engine faithful to that may make attributes feel as though they do not matter; an engine that makes them matter will fail it. Resolved: attribute effects are amplified for the game and the per-player residual band fails by design, the assumption that measured sizes would still feel real is rejected, and the cost falls on the assumption that the amplification stays out of the league, scoreline, and club bands.

Putting part of the quality gap in the repeat, so that a strong player has fewer bad days, argues with the measurement that finishing and saving barely repeat within a season, and with the chosen band on how far a team's worst match sits from its best; the assumption was that a consistency attribute could narrow a player's spread without moving the team's. Resolved: consistency acts on every action but by a different degree for each, which makes the departure from real data deliberate and graded, and a further assumption names the order the degrees follow.

Hiding a player's true attributes behind each club's scouting noise lets clubs disagree, but basing every transfer fee on a shared market valuation computed from the true attributes would tell every club the truth that scouting hid, so either the valuation comes from something else or the disagreement shrinks to each club's premium alone. Resolved: the shared valuation is built from visible data only (age, minutes, level, goals, recent fees, and reputation), so it never leaks the true attributes, and it is banded against real Transfermarkt valuations.

The new pressure-handling and sportsmanship traits describe much the same behaviour as the composure and aggression attributes the schema already carries, so the engine would either read two values for one behaviour or have to say what each value moves that the other does not. Resolved: each pair splits by scope, with the attribute acting on each action and the trait on occasions and choices.

Twelve hidden traits on the attribute scale, plus the wish for new performance attributes, met a schema that accepts 30 to 50 attributes in four fixed groups with 13 slots believed free; the traits alone would take 12 of the 13 and leave one slot for every new performance attribute. Resolved: personality becomes a fifth group with its own slots outside the limit.

Habits of play that act on their own, such as cutting inside, pull against the rule that the manager's instruction is always carried out as given: when an instruction to stay wide meets a habit of cutting inside, either the habit yields, which makes habits vanish under any instruction, or the habit wins, which weakens the instruction. Resolved: a strong habit wins sometimes, under pressure or low mood, and visibly, which amends the rule; the risk is that a player of the game reads this as the game ignoring the manager rather than as realism.
The realism test the engine plan already holds is three aggregate bands: goals per match from 2.4 to 3.2, shots per team from 8 to 16, and possession from 35 to 65 percent.
The realism test adds shape measures to the three aggregate bands: pass completion, where shots come from, possession in each third of the pitch, and goals by phase of play.
items.why: Three bands are not enough; with shape measures that the event stream already carries, a match that passes the bands and still looks wrong now fails something.

items.text: Calibration groups runs by condition (dry, wet, worn) and sets a band for each, so rain is expected to lower goals rather than to fail the test.
items.why: Pitch wear and weather interact, so the bands either had to hold across every combination of conditions or calibration would fix the conditions and never test them; a band per condition lets a condition move the numbers without failing the test.

items.text: The realism test reaches the season as well as the match: the shape of the league table, the shape of the market and of wages, and a watched season that a human reads and judges.
items.why: Transfers, wages, and budgets are the largest part of the product, and nothing tested whether a market, a wage bill, or a season of results reads as football; the person took every season measure offered.

items.text: A human watches matches as part of the realism test, as a milestone review rather than as a gate on every build.
items.why: The argument that justifies a person watching a season also justifies watching a match, and a watched match is the first instrument that can check whether a fully detailed model actually reads as football.

items.text: The realism test bands the spread as well as the average: how often a match finishes goalless, how often it finishes five-one, and how far a team's worst performance sits from its best.
items.why: Weak players swinging more and mood moving decisions both widen match-to-match variance, so the test has to measure the spread those mechanisms actually add.

items.text: Across 1826 matches in five top leagues in 2017/18, goals per match average 2.709 with a standard deviation of 1.675, and the distribution of total goals is Poisson to within 1.5 percentage points at every count, with a variance-to-mean ratio of 1.035.

Home teams score 1.530 goals a match and away teams 1.179, a home advantage of 0.351 goals, and results split 45.3 percent home wins, 24.5 percent draws, and 30.2 percent away wins (1826 matches, five leagues, 2017/18).

Per-match rates are tight across five different leagues: passes 839 to 888, pass accuracy 82.2 to 83.3 percent, shots 21.0 to 23.2, shot conversion 9.7 to 11.1 percent, duels 442 to 471, aerial duels 76 to 99, fouls 21 to 29, yellow cards 3.1 to 4.9, throw-ins 42 to 46, corners 9.5 to 10.3, goal kicks 16 to 17, free kicks 19 to 27, and offsides 4.0 to 5.0.

Mood, personality, and player quality change a team's scoring rate within a match and never the spread around it, so goals stay Poisson given that rate; the rule that a strong player differs from a weak one by fewer errors, a higher ceiling, and more consistency, and the rule that personality decides how strongly mood changes decisions, are both mechanisms for the rate rather than for the variance.
items.why: Real football's goal distribution is already Poisson, so the observed variance is fully explained by the scoring rate; extra variance would move the engine away from real football rather than towards it.

items.text: The realism test bands four things: the measured per-match rates across five leagues, the scoreline distribution and home advantage, pass completion as a curve by kind of pass and by pass length, and the physical output of players (distance covered, time at each speed, and peak sprint speed).
items.why: The planned three bands are several times wider than the real spread between leagues, so they would pass an engine that is visibly wrong; the person took all four families.

items.text: Shot conversion halves roughly every 5 metres: 51.9 percent inside 6 metres, 21.6 percent at 6 to 11, 12.2 percent at 11 to 16.5, 6.3 percent at 16.5 to 22, 2.8 percent at 22 to 30, and 1.8 percent beyond 30, measured over 40461 shots.

In provider-labelled tracking over 14 halves, the ball sits above half a metre for 29.6 percent of live play, above one metre for 23.9 percent, and above two metres for 17.1 percent, and it is in play for 55.4 percent of the match, so a strictly two-dimensional engine is wrong about a sixth of the live game.

Measured ball speed runs to a median of 6.47 metres per second, a ninety-ninth percentile of 24.9, and an extreme of 49.9, which confirms the earlier discard of a 57 metres per second reading as tracking noise and gives the engine a real speed ceiling in its place.

The official DFL live schema carries 31 event kinds and 139 distinct attributes at 1423 events a match, against the engine's four kinds carrying no player, no coordinates, and no outcome; the earlier estimate that the contract change means about fifteen event kinds plus a player, coordinates, and an outcome understates the gap by half on kinds and by a factor of forty on fields (7 DFL matches, 9961 events).

Whether a pass leaves the ground matters more than how far it travels: flat passes complete at 90.2 percent and high passes at 53.4, and a flat long pass completes at 68.6 percent while a high medium pass completes at 52.0, so the engine should branch on pass height before pass length.

Only about a third of shots reach the goalkeeper, because 38.4 percent go wide and 22.6 percent are blocked by a defender first, so a shot model that resolves attacker against goalkeeper models the minority case.

Data providers count the same action very differently: duels run at 64, 202, or 226 a match and through balls at 4.6, 15.6, or 44.1 depending on the provider, while providers that share a definition agree tightly, with carries of at least 5 metres at 287 against 273 (corrected from an earlier 271) and possession duration at 1.20 against 1.16 seconds; so every realism band must name the definition it copies.
The best player's season totals, such as the top scorer's goals and the most assists, stay inside the range real leagues produce, so the season realism test bands them.
items.why: It caps the deliberate amplification of player effects from the season side.

items.text: The realism test reads a separate, test-only output in which the engine writes per-player data; the event contract that the game reads stays as planned, and the rule that the contract gains its player identifier only when the season-layer work starts still holds.
items.why: The chosen bands need per-player data that the planned event contract does not carry, and a separate output lets the test run against the engine that ships without bringing the contract change forward.

items.text: The realism bands measured with StatsBomb definitions are converted to DFL definitions, one mapping per shared event kind, and the 7 public DFL matches check each conversion.
items.why: DFL definitions win for every shared event kind, but the public DFL set is only 7 matches, too few to measure most bands on its own; converting keeps the large StatsBomb sample of 200 matches.

items.text: The first watched-match review runs as soon as the first new mechanism runs, for example the choice model for when to shoot and which pass to pick, and a review follows each mechanism after it, so a failed mechanism is caught before other work builds on it.
items.why: A review run by hand only helps if it catches a failed mechanism before the rest of the model is built on it.

items.text: The watched-match reviewer uses all three comparisons: a simulated match side by side with a real match replayed in the same 2D view, a checklist of named qualities (shape, tempo, decisions, set pieces), and open judgement of what looks wrong.

The stream crate already serves a recorded fixture over the same protocol the viewer reads, at 50 ticks a second, so a real match converted into a fixture can play in the viewer beside a simulated one.

The realism test checks player development two ways: it bands what the research measured (peak age by position, speed of decline, conversion of youth players, and the after-effects of injury), and a person reads a set of simulated careers for what no band covers.
items.why: The person asked for the real data first, then chose to band what was measured and add watched careers, the same pattern as the season test.

items.text: The realism test checks finances two ways: it bands what the research measured (the revenue mix, the spread of broadcast income, league wage ratios, losses, transfer flows, and prize money), and a person reads a set of simulated club accounts for what no band covers.
items.why: The person asked for the real data first, then chose to band what was measured and add watched accounts, the same pattern as the career test.

items.text: The career test's injury band is re-sized on purpose to a softer target, and the game is banded against that target rather than against the real after-effects of a severe knee injury (a mean 216 days out, two seasons below par, and 20 percent of professional careers ended within three seasons).
items.why: The game deliberately carries severe injuries more gently than real football, with a shorter dip in form and no career ended by injury, so a band on real after-effects would fail by design.

items.text: Every band that departs from real football on purpose carries two numbers, the real target and a design target; the test passes on the design target and reports the distance from real data beside it, and this applies alike to the per-player band broken by the deliberate amplification of player effects, to the band for how consistency narrows each action, and to the softer injury band.
items.why: Otherwise a reader of the test would see one deliberate departure as a red failure and another as a green pass, with nothing to say that both are choices.

items.text: The realism test has measured joint bands: goals are Poisson once the club is known, with a within-club variance-to-mean ratio of 0.99, but shots are over-dispersed at 1.64 and crosses at 3.03; one team's shots run from 6 to 17 between the 10th and 90th percentiles, shots and goals correlate at only 0.32, and home and away shot counts correlate at minus 0.34 (1826 Wyscout league matches).

Only build steps that change play get a watched review, so the first review follows team shape and the defensive block, and the test harness and the player record are checked by numbers alone; this answers the ninth open question of the engine realism design document.

The design target for the deliberate amplification of player effects is that a top player looks clearly better than an average player in the same role in about two runs of five matches out of three, close to real football, so a manager needs more than one run to judge; this sets the size for the rule that a manager sees a better player over a run of about five matches.
items.why: It stays close to real football while still letting a manager see quality over a few runs.

items.text: The usual top scorer and top assister stay inside the real range, and a record season beyond it is possible about as rarely as real record seasons happen; this sets how strict the limit on the best player's season totals is, and the real range was still unmeasured when this was chosen.

Over about 20 seasons the league top scorer's goals run from 19 to 36 in the Premier League, 21 to 36 in Serie A, 16 to 41 in the Bundesliga, and 15 to 38 in Ligue 1, with medians of about 26 to 29, and LaLiga holds the outlier at Messi's 50 in 2011-12; the Premier League assist record is 21, and no source gives the tenth-best scorer's total.

The calibration sources carry different licences: the IDSSE DFL set and the Wyscout public set are CC-BY 4.0 and SkillCorner's open data is MIT, all usable commercially with attribution, while StatsBomb's open data is framed for research under a user agreement, Metrica's sample data has no formal licence, and the CC0 Transfermarkt dataset is scraped data that Transfermarkt's own terms and the EU database right may still cover.
items.evidence: https://github.com/spoho-datascience/idsse-data and https://figshare.com/collections/Soccer_match_event_dataset/4415000 and https://github.com/SkillCorner/opendata/blob/master/LICENSE and https://github.com/statsbomb/open-data (research sub-agent, batch 72)

items.text: The three aggregate calibration bands (goals, shots, and possession) are a sufficient test of realism.
The three calibration bands still hold once mood and personality move decisions; the extra variance does not push goals, shots, or possession outside them.
Aggregate shape measures can detect whether mood and personality read as football, and no human watches a match as part of the test.
A human can judge whether a simulated season reads as football from its table, its top scorers, and its transfer list, without watching any match inside it.
A milestone review that a person performs by hand catches what the shape measures miss, and it happens early enough to catch a failed mechanism before the rest of the model is built on it.
Real football publishes a distribution of scorelines and a team-to-team spread that the test can band against, the same way it published the three averages in the planned realism bands.
Goal-scoring in the engine can reproduce a Poisson distribution of total goals while mood, personality, and player quality all move the scoring rate.

Testing the physical bands (distance covered and time at each speed per outfield player, and the spread of peak sprint speed across a league) requires the engine to report per-player distance and speed, which the engine does not report today.
Ball height costs the engine little, because crates/engine/src/ball.rs already carries a third axis and a third velocity component, so the work is in the rules rather than in the state.

The engine can carry a provider-grade event contract with a core of five fields (player, team, x, y, outcome) on every on-ball event, adding per-kind qualifiers only for the kinds the realism tests read, rather than reproducing all 139 attributes of the official DFL schema.

The realism test bands each action family against one named provider definition, StatsBomb for most on-ball and goalkeeper actions, SkillCorner for runs and pressing, and DFL tracking for carries, shielding, and goalkeeper positioning, rather than mixing definitions within a band.

The deliberate amplification of player effects can be confined to player-level outcomes, so the league bands (goals, home advantage, and per-match rates), the Poisson scoreline, and the club-to-club spread band still pass while only the per-player residual band fails.
One amplification size exists that is large enough for a manager to see a better player over about five matches and small enough for the best player's season totals to stay inside the real range.

The realism test checks the style clash by fitting the measured possession rule (match possession equals 0.487 plus 0.949 times the difference in the two clubs' season means, plus 0.027 at home) across every simulated match with AI managers on both sides, and the fitted multiplier lands near 0.949; the person gave no preference on the test, so this follows from the decision that the rule is an output of the matches and not an input, rather than from a choice.
Each StatsBomb definition has a DFL equivalent close enough to convert a band, and 7 DFL matches are enough to check the conversion even where they are too few to measure the band.
DFL tracking at 25 frames a second converts into a fixture of 50-tick frames by interpolation, with player identities mapped to shirt numbers, and the viewer shows it without a change to the viewer.

The realism bands measured on StatsBomb open data can still calibrate a commercial game, because calibration uses derived statistics rather than shipping the data; StatsBomb's research framing makes this a question for StatsBomb, not a settled right.

Per-player form pulled against an event contract that carried no player identifier, and the stream-protocol slice was already complete with four slices depending on it, so per-player form needed the same kind of costly contract change already named for the player record. Resolved: the event contract changes when the work to build the season layer starts, with the assumption that the later migration cost is acceptable; the decision covers the event contract only, so the question of when the player record changes stayed open.

Transfers, wages, and budgets are part of the product, yet the only realism test was the match bands with their shape measures, so nothing tested whether a market, a wage bill, or a season of results reads as football and the largest part of the product had no realism test. Resolved: the season test takes all three measures, table shape, market and wage shape, and a watched season.

The season test put a human in the loop while the match test kept a human out, yet the argument that justifies watching a season justifies watching a match. Resolved: the assumption that aggregates alone can judge a match fell, and a person now watches matches too, as a milestone review rather than a gate on every build.

The board handled a deliberate departure from real football two ways: the per-player band kept real data and failed by design under the amplification of player effects, while the injury band moved to a softer target and passed, so a reader saw one choice as a red failure and the other as a green pass. Resolved: every departed band carries a real target and a design target, passes on the design target, and reports its distance from real data.

Most realism bands are converted from 200 StatsBomb matches, and transfer fees and valuations are banded against the Transfermarkt-derived career dataset, but StatsBomb's open data is framed for research and the Transfermarkt set is exposed to Transfermarkt's own terms, so two of the test's largest sources may not be usable in a commercial game, while the event contract has already removed the same risk by using the game's own names with a mapping to outside schemas. Resolved: you accept the risk, and the bands keep their current sources.

The board believed the engine bounced the ball off the touchlines and the goal lines like walls, with no throw-ins, corners, goal kicks, or offside. The code now shows otherwise: the protocol's event list (crates/protocol/src/event.rs) carries throw-in, corner, goal-kick, and offside events.

items.text: Every realism band is an output that the mechanisms must produce, never a value the engine is tuned to hit directly. The watched-match reviews catch what the bands miss (a review after each new mechanism, where the reviewer compares a simulated match with a real match replayed in the same 2D view, works through a checklist of named qualities, and judges openly what looks wrong), and a failed review reopens the question of whether more detail in the planned model produces football that reads as real.
items.why: Asked how to settle whether more detail produces real-looking football, the person chose a principle plus the watched review rather than waiting for a proof.

items.text: The planned tactics model is Tier 2: a formation, a mentality, six team instructions, and a role and duty for each player, as written in the tactics-and-AI slice of the match-engine workflow.

The person's thought is three readings at once: the planned model needs more detail inside it, the numbers can pass while the football is still missing, and the realism test is too weak to catch either.
items.why: Asked which reading of the realism gap was theirs, the person answered with a mix of readings rather than a single one.

items.text: This board runs ahead of the build: the football-manager-match-engine workflow is at the plan and implement stages of its stream-protocol slice, so every candidate here lands as later scope and none corrects work already in flight.
The match-engine build workflow places leagues, seasons, competitions, transfers, and finances out of scope, and it parks injury persistence because no season model exists.
The tactic has two phases, in possession and out of possession, each with its own shape and its own instructions, so the formation becomes two formations and the switch between them needs timing.
Set pieces are designed routines with assigned takers, and the opponent sets a defensive routine against them, so a set piece is a duel rather than a dice roll.

Tier 3 is per-player instructions and opposition instructions together, plus manager-set triggers for pressing, the defensive line, and similar situations. The person added the triggers themselves; they were not among the options offered.
Every idea on this board belongs to a second workflow, a realism programme started separately from the match-engine workflow already in flight.
items.why: Form and season context need a season model that the engine workflow excludes, so the ideas are kept out of the build in flight.

items.text: The distillation produces several candidates split by dependency, one per coherent piece, rather than one large candidate.
items.why: So the cheapest pieces can start first.

items.text: The stream-protocol slice is complete and four later slices depend on it, so the event contract is a second completed contract, after the player record, that the realism work wants changed.

The realism work splits into two programmes: engine realism (the player as a person, the club and squad, Tier 3 tactics, conditions and officials, the rebuilt realism test, and both managers as entities) and the season layer that earns form. The engine-facing pieces start while the season layer is still being shaped.
items.why: The season layer had grown into a full management game with a calendar, cups, a table, and season-long availability, larger than the engine it was meant to follow, so one second workflow no longer fitted.

items.text: Touchline is one product, a football-management game, and the match engine is its first component; the workflow in flight is stage one of a longer programme rather than the whole thing.

The match-engine workflow in flight keeps its charter and its exclusions unchanged. The exclusions describe that workflow correctly even though they no longer describe the product, and splitting the work into an engine-realism programme and a season-layer programme is what keeps both statements true.
items.why: The exclusions still describe that workflow correctly, and the two-programme split keeps both descriptions true, so the work in flight pays nothing.

items.text: The engine is done when a person can watch and manage one match from start to finish, exactly as the sixteen-slice roster describes; calling the product a football-management game does not change the engine's definition of done.

Real phase-of-play data uses nine paired phases rather than two: build-up, create, finish, direct, transition, quick break, set play, chaotic, and disruption, each locked one-to-one to the opponent's high block, medium block, low block, and the matching defending phases. Measured on SkillCorner data from 20 A-League matches of 2024/25.

The two phases differ by a measurable amount: in possession a team is 46 to 49 metres wide with a defensive line 34 to 37 metres up the pitch, and out of possession 36 to 38 metres wide with the line at 31 to 35 metres, while depth barely changes. Measured on Metrica tracking and event data from 2 matches at 25 frames per second.
The manager authors two phases and the engine derives which of the nine paired phases it is in from its own state, so the tactic interface stays at two while the model runs nine.
items.why: It keeps the tactic interface simple while the model still runs the nine phases that real data shows.

items.text: The shape does not move uniformly between phases: on broadcast tracking from 20 matches (3.87 million samples), when a team wins the ball the back line advances about 3.5 metres while full-backs, wing-backs, and wingers advance 9 to 12 metres, so the team stretches from the back rather than sliding. Ground-truth tracking later halved these magnitudes and reversed the back line's direction.

The block tracks the ball at a fixed ratio, about 0.63 metres up the pitch for every metre the ball advances and 0.30 to 0.39 metres sideways for every metre it moves across, with the same slope in and out of possession; what changes between phases is width, 45.1 metres in possession against 35.4 out of it. Measured on SkillCorner broadcast data from 20 matches (1.76 million team-frames).

Only 1.62 of the twenty outfielders stand within 5 metres of the ball and 3.71 within 10, the ten-metre zone is balanced at 1.84 attackers to 1.87 defenders, and 51.5 percent of live frames hold at most one player inside 5 metres, so the ball is uncontested more often than it is contested (2 Bundesliga matches, 154 thousand live frames). These figures were corrected after a position-code fix restored two wingers; the first version read 1.55, 3.55, 1.77 to 1.78, and 54.8 percent.

Ground-truth tracking confirms the block law first measured on broadcast data: the team centroid moves 0.558 metres up the pitch per metre of ball advance in possession and 0.555 out of it, and 0.35 and 0.39 sideways, staying within 0.44 to 0.68 across 52 team-halves from 7 German league (DFL) matches, while width changes from 46.1 metres in possession to 36.8 out and depth changes by under 3 metres.

Ground-truth tracking corrects the broadcast finding that the back line advances about 3.5 metres and the wide players 9 to 12 metres when a team wins the ball. The ordering survives, with wide midfielders advancing 7.4 metres and full-backs 5.5 against a centre-back's zero, but the magnitudes halve and the back line moves the other way: the deepest outfielder drops 1.4 metres deeper while the centroid advances 2.5, so the team stretches rather than sliding forward (52 team-halves, 7 DFL matches).

Both managers decide live: the AI manager changes its tactic during the match, the human can pause and change as well, and the human's pre-set triggers for pressing, the defensive line, and similar situations are an extra tool rather than the only one. The code confirms the protocol already queues a tactics change or a substitution during a match (crates/protocol/src/command.rs); the AI side is not yet verified.
items.evidence: crates/protocol/src/command.rs:1 and crates/protocol/src/command.rs:11 (the change queue; the AI side is unverified)

items.text: A set-piece routine changes four things: who wins first contact, where the ball goes (near post, far post, or short), where players stand for the second ball, and how many stay back against the counter.
items.why: Real corner data shows a set piece is decided by first contact, so the routine's levers are sized around it.

items.text: Every live change, tactical or a substitution, takes effect at the next stoppage, for both managers; the plan already applies each queued change at a qualifying stoppage through the match-rules slice, so pausing gives the human time to think but no earlier effect.

The manager sets two team transition choices, to counter-press or drop back on losing the ball and to counter-attack or keep the ball on winning it, and each player carries an own transition instruction as a Tier 3 per-player instruction, which defaults sensibly from the team choices until the manager changes it.
The manager sees the nine derived phases after the match only: the post-match report shows time spent in each phase and how the team did in each, and the match view does not show the current phase.

The engine-realism programme builds team shape and the block first, following the measured law that the team slides with the ball and changes width by phase, so the first watched-match review judges the cheapest mechanism that changes how every match looks.
items.why: It is the cheapest mechanism that changes how every match looks, so the first review judges something visible early.

items.text: The season-layer piece of work no longer stays one card: it splits into smaller cards that can each start on their own, and the split is written at the next distillation.

Engine realism runs first and the season layer follows, as the decisions to put the realism work in a second workflow and to split it into two programmes already set it, so the four season cards (competitions, squad and careers, the market, and club business) build on a realistic match.
items.why: So the season cards build on a match that is already realistic.

items.text: The card that asked when the player record changes shape becomes a recorded decision rather than a card, because the board already answered it: the record changes when the realism programme starts. The card to rebuild the realism test is rewritten at the next distillation to the test the board now holds: bands for per-match rates, scorelines and home advantage, pass completion, and physical output; a separate test-only output with per-player data; one internal match record behind both outputs; a watched-match review after each new mechanism with three comparisons; and bands plus a person's reading for player development and for club finances.
items.why: The player-record question was already answered, so it needs no investigation run, and the realism-test card no longer matched what the board had decided.

items.text: Goals come from both short and long possessions: possessions of 0 to 2 passes give 34 percent of goals and possessions of 10 or more give 25; a ball won in the final third leads to a shot 27.0 percent of the time against 9.7 in the own third; 34.1 percent of the 200 open-play losses a match are regained within 5 seconds; and a SkillCorner quick break leads to a shot 46 percent of the time. Measured on 200 StatsBomb matches and 20 SkillCorner matches.
items.evidence: .scratch/out/gap_sb.txt (200 StatsBomb matches) and FINDINGS.md §16; verified .scratch/out/gap_sc.txt (20 SkillCorner matches) and FINDINGS.md §16

items.text: Pressing has measured triggers and the block a measured shape: a player receiving a forward pass is engaged 88.5 percent of the time against 59.5 after a backward pass, 78 percent when wide against 56 in the centre, and 82 percent against a low block; the defending block keeps a near-constant length of about 30 metres, its last defender advancing 0.49 metres and its midfield line 0.61 per metre of ball advance. Measured on 20 SkillCorner matches and 7 DFL matches with tracking joined to events.

items.text: Marking tightens near goal and hands over quickly: the nearest defending outfielder stands a median 2.4 metres from an attacker in the box-depth zone against 6.3 metres far from goal, and the nearest defender is still the same player 5 seconds later 64.0 percent of the time overall but only 51.3 percent near goal and 37.8 percent over 10 seconds. Measured on 7 DFL matches with tracking joined to events.
items.evidence: .scratch/out/gap_idsse_an.txt (7 DFL matches, tracking joined to events) and FINDINGS.md §16

items.text: Set pieces are first-contact contests: a corner leads to a goal 3.45 percent of the time and to a shot 38.0 percent, the attacking team wins first contact on 37.2 percent of long corners and then shoots 68.9 percent of the time against 20.5 when the defenders win it, corners, free kicks, and penalties together give 36 percent of goals, and a direct free kick scores 3.2 percent of the time. Measured on 200 StatsBomb matches.
The plans already in progress are the floor, so every idea on this board adds scope and none removes planned scope.
Adding more detail inside the planned model produces the emergent football that is missing when the numbers pass but the match still does not read like football.
A manager-set trigger can live in the rule pack and the change queue, so no conditional tactic logic enters the engine's tick loop.

The charter of the football-manager-match-engine workflow still describes that workflow correctly, although the product is now read as a management game and the charter records exclusions (leagues, seasons, competitions, transfers, and finances) that the product no longer honours.
Nine paired phases can be derived from the engine's own state rather than authored by the manager, so the tactic interface stays at two phases while the model runs nine.

A team's block can be made to track the ball at the fixed measured ratio (about 0.63 metres up the pitch and 0.30 to 0.39 metres sideways per metre the ball moves) without explicit per-player marking logic in the tick loop.

The AI manager's live decisions enter the match through the same change queue as the human's, so both sides change tactics the same way and no tactic logic runs inside the tick loop; this extends the assumption about manager-set triggers to every live change.

A per-player transition default can be derived from the team's two transition choices and the player's role and attributes, so a manager who never opens the per-player screen still gets a coherent team transition.

One reading treats the planned model as the right shape that only needs more detail; another says a fully detailed model can still pass the numbers without reading like football, so more detail does not imply emergence. The proposed bridge, personality deciding how strongly the player's own mood and the team's mood change that player's decisions, was never tested; putting a human in front of a match as a milestone review made it checkable, on the assumption that such a review catches the failure in time. Resolved by a principle rather than a proof: every realism band is an output the mechanisms must produce, never a tuned value, a failed watched-match review reopens this tension, and the bet that more detail produces emergent football stands.

Form, season context, and a manager who moves form all need the season model that the engine build workflow excludes. Resolved: a season layer came into scope and was placed in a second workflow, so the assumption that form and season context could be supplied as asserted numbers in the team file was rejected, and the numbers are earned rather than asserted.

Giving each player a competence rating for every position changes the shape of the player record, the data-schemas slice that defines that record is already complete, and the realism workflow starts only after the engine ships; the change is cheapest before the engine is built on the record, so this order pays a migration cost instead. Resolved: following the precedent set for the event contract, the record changes when the realism programme starts, on the assumption that migrating the match-rules and tactics-and-AI slices later costs less than delaying them now. The question of when the player record changes shape is answered and needs no investigation run.

Putting all the realism work in one second workflow that starts after the engine ships pulled against making that workflow a full football-management game with a calendar, cups, a table, and season-long availability, larger than the engine it was meant to follow. The assumption that the season layer would never change the engine's data contract also failed, because team and per-player form and the combined club calendar and squad availability both want data the engine does not emit. Resolved: the work splits into two programmes, engine realism and the season layer, which rejects the assumption that one second workflow still fits; the no-contract-change assumption is rejected too, because the event contract is now changed after the fact by design rather than by accident.

The product is a football-management game whose first component is the engine, while the engine workflow's own charter excludes leagues, seasons, competitions, transfers, and finances; the workflow in flight was building to a charter the product has outgrown, and nothing had told it. Resolved: the charter stays as it stands and the engine's definition of done is unchanged, because splitting the work into two programmes makes both descriptions true at once, which confirms that the charter still describes its own workflow. The residual cost is that a reader of that workflow alone will take the engine for the whole product.

The event-contract change was deferred to the realism programme and priced as adding a player identifier, but real provider data puts its true size at roughly fifteen event types instead of four (a real match carries about 1683 events; Wyscout uses 10 types and about 35 subtypes and kloppy's model 19 types), plus a player identifier, coordinates, and an outcome on every event. The deferral was priced as one field and is really a redesign of the contract. Resolved: the programme accepts the full redesign and copies a real provider schema in full, so the core-subset idea (player, team, x, y, and outcome with a few per-kind qualifiers) is rejected and the cost is priced at its true size.

A team file today carries a club identifier, a name, a short name, and two kit colours; it carries no reputation, no home ground, and no crowd data, so two clubs differ only in their players and every fixture is played on neutral ground.
A team carries a mood of its own, separate from the mood of each player.
Team mood is moved by match events, by the score and the clock together, by the crowd and the venue, and by the context before the match.
Team mood is also moved by recent form, by the season so far, and by team context such as a club known for late goals or for slumps.
The manager is an entity with attributes of their own, and those attributes affect the team's form and mood.
Team mood shifts how players behave inside the chosen tactic and gates the error rate; it does not change the tactic itself.
The club carries a home ground with a home advantage, a reputation and stature, a squad familiarity value for each tactic, and a playing identity.
The squad has leadership, partnerships between pairs of players, and a cohesion value; cohesion is measured for the whole squad and again for the eleven on the pitch.

Both managers carry attributes, and a manager weak at tactics has their instructions land weaker on the pitch, so the human player's own competence becomes part of the simulation. This mechanism was later replaced by the rule that an instruction is always carried out as given, with a weak tactician making poor choices instead.
items.why: The person wanted both managers to carry attributes that matter, so that the player's own competence is part of the simulation.

items.text: The share of time the ball is above 1 metre differs between competitions, 12.4 percent in European elite matches against 19.4 percent in the A-League (measured on 20 SkillCorner A-League matches from 2024/25), so ball height is a measurable signal of playing identity rather than a constant.

Club-to-club style varies far more than league-to-league: across 98 clubs in 1826 Wyscout matches from five leagues, pass accuracy spans 73 to 90 percent against 1.1 percentage points between leagues, pass volume varies 2.57 times, mean pass length spans 17.9 to 23.0 metres, and shot conversion spans 4.9 to 17.5 percent.

Physical output separates neither divisions nor clubs: in seven DFL matches (247 full player-halves tracked at 25 frames per second), Bundesliga outfielders cover 110.0 metres per minute against 115.4 in the second division, top speed and sprint share are identical between the divisions, and across fourteen team-matches the spread is 20 percent, against the 73 to 90 percent club-to-club spread in pass accuracy measured across 98 clubs.
items.evidence: .scratch/out/idsse_players.csv (7 DFL matches, 247 full player-halves at 25 fps)

items.text: A club's style has three layered sources: a club identity that survives a change of manager, the squad's own abilities, and the manager's tactic, and each adds its own part to how the club plays.
items.why: It produces the large club-to-club variation in style that the realism test must check and that nothing on the board produced before.

items.text: When two styles meet, the measured additive possession rule (match possession equals 0.487 plus 0.949 times the difference in the two clubs' season means, plus 0.027 at home) is the default, and the manager's tactic for that match moves the result away from it, so a possession club may choose to give the ball up in one match; the realism test bands the default. The Wyscout data verifies the default rule only; the effect of the tactic is unverified, and the default was later made an emergent output rather than a rule applied to each match.
items.evidence: .scratch/out/gap_wy.txt:166 (the default rule only; the tactic effect is unverified)

items.text: The measured additive possession rule is an output, not an input: tactic, squad, and identity drive each match, one match may land far from the rule, and the season results must reproduce it. This amends the earlier reading that applied the rule as each match's default, so the default is now emergent rather than applied.
items.why: After a worked example, the person read the measured rule as the average: it was measured on real clubs whose managers already chose a tactic for every match, so adding a tactic on top of it would count that adaptation twice.

items.text: An AI manager picks each match tactic from four inputs: its own philosophy, the opponent's strength and style, the match state by score and clock, and the season situation such as table position, a cup match, or a tired squad.

No instruction lands weaker because of the manager; a manager weak at tactics makes poor tactical choices and understands the match poorly instead. This replaces the earlier mechanism in which a weak manager's instructions landed weaker, and the instruction a manager gives is always carried out as given.
items.why: The person corrected the earlier mechanism: there are no weak instructions, only poor choices, because a player told that their own instructions land weaker would read it as the game ignoring them rather than as realism.

items.text: The human manager's tactical attribute acts on three things and never on an instruction: how accurate the manager's information is (opposition reports, match analysis, and scouting noise, the same noisy estimate of attributes a club's scouting produces), how fast the squad learns a new tactic (the squad's familiarity value for each tactic), and how the squad's mood and trust respond to the manager's choices over time.
items.why: The human player makes the human manager's choices, so once a weak tactician meant poor choices, the human's tactical attribute had nothing left to act on; the person chose these three things for it.

items.text: A squad that distrusts a weak manager makes more errors after the same instruction, and that is mood rather than a weakened instruction: the instruction is carried out as given and the players carry it out worse, so the rule that an instruction is always carried out as given stays true.
items.why: The person judged it acceptable because the extra errors come from mood, not from the instruction itself.

items.text: Substitutions follow the score: across 1826 Wyscout league matches in 2017/18 a team makes 2.85 changes per match at median minutes 61, 72, and 82, a team that trails makes its first change at minute 57 against 66 for a team that leads, midfielders are half of the players taken off, and only 6.5 percent of changes happen at half time.

Team strength has a measured size in 1826 Wyscout league matches: the best attack in a league scores about twice the league average and the worst about 0.6 times it, the home factor runs from 1.19 to 1.35, 71 to 84 percent of the spread in points per game is team quality, a top-quarter club beats a bottom-half club 71.0 percent of the time and loses 10.4 percent, and evenly matched games draw 4 to 6 points more often than two independent Poisson scorers predict.

Club style has two layers: one axis carries 59 percent of style variance and is mostly strength, with possession correlating 0.74 with points per game, while crosses and take-ons are almost independent of strength. The opponent sets match possession as much as the club does, since match possession equals 0.487 plus 0.949 times the difference in the two clubs' season means plus 0.027 at home, and a club's possession swings 10.3 points from match to match against a 7.2-point spread between clubs (1826 Wyscout league matches).

Quality scales as small execution gaps in every family of action: seven DFL matches show no measurable gap between the Bundesliga and the 2. Bundesliga, while inside one league (1826 Wyscout matches) the top quarter of clubs beats its situational expectation by 1.7 points of pass completion, 2.0 of shot conversion, and 2.5 in duels and take-ons, and the bottom quarter falls short by 1.2, 2.1, and 1.2.
items.evidence: .scratch/out/gap_wy.txt (1826 Wyscout league matches) and FINDINGS.md §16; verified .scratch/out/gap_div.txt

items.text: Session 5 first clears the open questions that block the first build steps, and then it opens the areas no session has covered.
Four areas are missing realism the board never covered: the staff around the squad, contracts and the dressing room, supporters and the press, and international football.

The attribute schema holds 36 attributes, nine in each of the four groups, so 14 slots are free. The board's earlier readings of 37 attributes and 13 free slots are out of date, and the first open question of the engine realism design document is answered.

The match event now carries 17 event types and an optional player identifier and second player identifier. The board's earlier readings (that the event carries only kick-off, goal, full-time, and tactics-change with no player identifier, and that throw-ins, corners, goal kicks, and offside do not exist) are out of date, so the event contract redesign starts from a larger contract than the board records.

The player's own match plays in real time, or as its key moments only, so the manager can act as it happens; every other match stays a full simulation, and realism comes before speed, so the programme sets no speed limit up front.
items.why: The person put realism first when asked how long they may wait.

items.text: The other matches of a matchday simulate in the background while the player watches their own match, so the results are ready at the final whistle and live scores from other grounds appear as they happen.

Key moments come in tiers that together cover four kinds: chances and goals, moments the manager may act on (a tiring player, an injury, a card, a change of shape), a filter the manager sets, and the moments that tell the story of the result, including pressure that produced no shot.
After the questions that block the first three build steps, session 5 stays on the open questions of the later build steps before it opens any new area.

Until the season layer exists, each test match sets form, table position, and the season situation by hand, so the mood mechanism and the AI manager can be tested in extreme states such as a relegation fight.
items.why: The season layer that would supply these values does not exist yet.

items.text: The technical open questions of the event contract design document (serialisation, kind names on the wire, the Delete record, freeze-frame scope, the change-queue fields, the envelope version, and the keeper kinds) are questions for the plan of that build step, not for this board.

Form, season context, and a club's reputation for late goals can be supplied as asserted numbers in the team file, with no season model behind them. Rejected: these inputs now come from the season layer.
The manager is a modelled entity with attributes, and not only the AI module the shape document already names.

Partnership data for each pair of players can be generated for a squad of 22 without a shared history to derive it from. Rejected: the season layer instead generates a backstory of past seasons when a new save is created, so partnerships start from a shared history.
Players of the game accept that their own instructions land weaker when their manager is weak at tactics, and read the loss of authority as realism rather than as the game ignoring them.
The engine can keep club identity, squad, and tactic as separate inputs to style, so the realism test can check a club-to-club spread band and still tell which layer produced the spread.

AI managers that pick tactics from their four inputs (philosophy, opponent, match state, and season situation) produce, over a season, choices whose results reproduce the measured possession rule with its 0.949 multiplier, so the rule emerges as an output without being tuned directly.

The three effects of the tactical attribute (information accuracy, learning speed for a new tactic, and the squad's mood and trust response) apply to AI managers as well as to the human, so both sides of a match are modelled the same way and only the source of the choices differs.
A player of the game can tell mood-driven errors from an ignored instruction, because the squad's mood and trust are visible to the manager before and during the match.
The other matches of a matchday fit in the background of a real-time match on the player's machine without slowing the player's own match or its view.

A player of the game reads a habit that overrides an instruction under pressure as realism, because the match view or the report names the habit and the moment, and not as the game ignoring the manager. This is, in a narrower form, the same risk as the rejected bet that players would accept instructions landing weaker under a weak manager.

The realism test bands league-wide per-match rates to about one percentage point, yet the club-to-club spread on the same statistic is 17 points; because the test adopted the league bands alone, it would pass an engine in which every club plays identically, and nothing on the board produced club variation of that size. The measured size of team strength and the split of club style into a strength axis and a pure-style layer supplied the band, and it was resolved by building club style from three layers (identity, squad, and tactic), at the cost of keeping those layers separate in the engine.

Adding the manager's match tactic on top of the measured additive possession rule, with the rule banded as the default, pulled against how the rule was measured: the 0.949 multiplier comes from real clubs whose managers already chose a tactic for every match, so an engine that adds a tactic on top counts that adaptation twice. Resolved by making the rule an output of the matches rather than an input to them, so no tactic is counted twice.

Both managers carry attributes, and a weak tactician is one who makes poor choices; the AI manager's choices come from its attributes, but the human player makes the human manager's choices, so the human manager's tactical attribute had nothing left to act on. Resolved by giving the attribute three things to act on (information accuracy, learning speed, and squad reaction), none of which is the instruction.

The rule that an instruction is always carried out as given removes every path by which a manager weakens an instruction, yet the manager's attribute moves squad mood and trust, and team mood gates the error rate, so a weak manager's team makes more errors after the same instruction: the removed weakening arriving by a longer road. Resolved by reading those errors as mood rather than a weakened instruction, so the rule stays true; the remaining risk is whether a player of the game can tell the two apart.
The licence risk of the StatsBomb and Transfermarkt sources is accepted: the realism test keeps its current sources, because it uses derived statistics and the game ships none of the data.
items.why: You are not worried about the risk, so no band is measured again on other data.

items.text: Each band records the data set it was measured on, so a band can be measured again on another set later at low cost if the licence position ever changes.
The fast result-only model passes the same season bands as the full engine: points spread, goals, home advantage, and draw share.
items.why: A result-only league must not look easier or harder than an active one.

items.text: Creating a new save may take a few minutes, with a progress view that shows the past seasons as they finish.
items.why: History depth and every UEFA league are worth a short wait at the start.

items.text: The realism test bands the cup upset rate: how often a lower-division club beats a higher one, by the gap in divisions, measured from openfootball and Wikipedia results.
items.why: A cup tie is a match, so the match bands already cover play; what cups add is the upset.

items.text: The money bands and the game's accounts use euros, and the player picks the currency the screens show.
items.why: One currency inside removes the pounds-and-euros mix from every band, and the player still sees a familiar currency.

items.text: The fast model can simulate several past seasons of every UEFA league inside a few minutes on the player's machine.
Which cups and which seasons give the upset-rate band, and how the band treats a cup that seeds its draw or gives the lower club home advantage.
Which exchange rate converts a pound figure to euros for each season of a band.
Staff are people who also carry a rating: coaches, scouts and analysts, medical and sports-science staff, the assistant manager, a director of football, and other football roles beyond these.
items.why: Every one of these roles changes what the manager knows or what the squad can do, and a rating gives a quick read of a person you still get to know.

items.text: Staff have a personality, with opinions, temper, and loyalty, so they can clash with the manager and with players.
items.why: A star rating with no person behind it feels wrong.

items.text: Staff have trade-offs: a coach has specialisms, for example good with young players and poor with veterans, so a better coach is not better at everything.
items.why: A rating that is always better removes the choice.

items.text: Staff have a market: they cost real wages, other clubs can poach them, and they can follow a manager to a new club.
items.why: Staff that never move are not part of the football world.

items.text: Staff have a voice: they advise and warn, for example a physio who says a player is close to injury.
items.why: A real manager hears the staff before deciding.

items.text: The game also employs the wider staff of a real club: a sport psychologist, a nutritionist, strength and conditioning and rehabilitation coaches, a head groundsman, a team manager for travel and matchday logistics, a welfare officer and a translator for new signings, a loan manager, a head of recruitment, data scientists, and a set-piece analyst.
items.why: Several of these roles act on mechanisms already on the board, for example the groundsman on pitch wear and the psychologist on mood.

items.text: Every staff role is a person, with attributes, a personality, a contract, and a career.
items.why: A department level would bring back the rating that feels wrong.

items.text: Every staff role as a person, in every club of every UEFA league, means tens of thousands of staff to generate and simulate, which pulls against a save that starts in a few minutes and a fast model that runs most leagues with results only. Resolved: staff are full people only in the active leagues, and a light record elsewhere becomes full when it matters.

Staff are full people only in the active leagues; a club in a result-only league holds a light record of each staff member, which becomes a full person when it matters, for example when an active club hires that person or the league becomes active.
items.why: Full staff everywhere would break the save that starts in a few minutes.

items.text: Staff numbers and staff quality differ by league, division, and tier, as they do in real football, so a lower-division club employs fewer and less specialised staff than a top club.
items.why: A fourth-tier club with fifty specialists would not be real.

items.text: The player chooses, department by department, whether to hire staff directly or to delegate the hiring to the head of that department.
items.why: Hiring fifty people by hand suits some players and not others.

items.text: Staff advice reaches the manager through three channels: written reports and messages, a word from the assistant and the analysts during the match, and regular staff meetings where heads of department raise concerns and proposals.
items.why: A real manager hears staff in all three ways, and advice only on request would hide the staff.

items.text: Staff advice can be wrong in four ways: random error that shrinks with quality, a personal leaning from personality that the manager can learn, the staff member's own agenda, and blind spots outside the specialism.
items.why: Real advice is wrong in personal ways, and learning each person's leanings is part of the manager's job.

items.text: Overruling the staff has consequences: an ignored staff member can become unhappy and leave, players hear about clashes and the team mood moves, and the game remembers who was right, so trust grows or falls with the record.
items.why: A final word that costs nothing would make the staff's voice empty.

items.text: The manager designs the set-piece routines and may delegate the design to the set-piece coach; the coach's quality decides how well and how fast the players learn the routines and how many routines the squad can run properly.
items.why: The routine is the manager's idea, but the coach decides how well it reaches the players.

items.text: Fitness and sports-science staff move how fast players tire and how much the team fades late in a match.
items.why: The match changes with the clock, and fitness work is the staff's mark on that change.

items.text: Analysts find the opponent's habits, and the quality of their work decides how well the opposition instructions land.
items.why: An opposition instruction is only as good as the analysis behind it.

items.text: Coaches drill the shape and the pressing, so a new tactic takes time to learn and good coaches shorten that time.
items.why: A tactic that works at full strength on the first day is not real.

items.text: Each staff member carries a playing idea: staff whose idea fits the club's style get more out of the players, and staff whose idea clashes with the manager's tactic work less well and complain.
items.why: Real clubs hire staff to fit a style, and a new manager often brings staff who share the idea.

items.text: A squad can run only a limited number of set-piece routines properly, and the limit is a design value, because no public data measures it.

Staff headcount falls steeply by tier: a Bundesliga club employs about 350 full-time staff and a 2. Bundesliga club about 158, so a second-tier club has about 45 percent of a top-tier club's staff (DFL, 2024/25). A European top-division club averages about 130 full-time-equivalent staff (UEFA, 2024), while large Premier League clubs employ 600 to more than 1,200 people.

Specialist roles fall off steeply below the top: a top club runs a median of 5 match analysts and 3 sports scientists (32 clubs, 2024); full-time nutritionists work at 14 of 26 Category 1 English academies and at 1 of 63 lower-category academies; and only 14 percent of English non-league clubs have a sports scientist and 4 percent a nutritionist.
items.evidence: https://www.tandfonline.com/doi/full/10.1080/24733938.2024.2341837 and https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/35300580/ and https://doi.org/10.3390/app15031050 (research sub-agent, batch 81)

items.text: Performance staff pay falls by division: Premier League fitness and sports-science staff earn about 6,300 pounds more than Championship staff and about 21,800 pounds more than League Two staff (138 staff surveyed, about 2023). Non-player wages across UEFA top-division clubs reached 5.2 billion euros in 2024, with no split by tier.

About three coaches leave with each sacked manager: in one recent English season about 150 coaches lost their jobs alongside about 50 dismissed managers. Some managers bring five or more assistants to a new club, and others hire new staff at each club. No study gives the share of staff who move with a manager, and the season of the English figure needs a check.

No published figures give average staff headcount for English divisions below the Premier League or for the 3. Liga, how common set-piece coaches, loan managers, or data scientists are by division, or non-player wages by tier.

Staff follow a manager in four ways at once: each manager has a trusted inner circle that grows over a career; each staff member decides by personality and by the bond with the manager; the old club can block a move or ask for compensation while a contract runs; and the player's own manager can bring trusted staff to a new club.
items.why: About three coaches leave with each sacked manager, and the movement is personal.

items.text: Staff can be poached: a staff member weighs club size, pay, role, and ambition; a club that takes staff under contract pays compensation; staff can leave for a promotion, for example to a head-coach post; and the player can approach other clubs' staff under the same rules.
items.why: Losing a good coach to a bigger club is part of real football.

items.text: Staff have careers: attributes grow with experience and fall with age; retired players can start as coaches or scouts and carry traits from their playing days; assistants and coaches can become AI managers, so the manager pool grows out of the staff; and staff build a reputation from results and the players they develop, which sets their market value.
items.why: Staff are people, so they need a past and a future as players do.

items.text: What the staff rating shows, and whether each club sees it exactly or through its own judgment.
Each club sees a staff member's rating through its own judgment, so the rating can be wrong, as a scouting report on a player can.
items.why: Staff are seen the same way players are, so no club sees the truth for free.

items.text: Staff carry four more things: knowledge of leagues, regions, and languages that sets where their judgment is sharp; bonds with players, who play better for coaches they trust and may follow them; a workload, so overloaded staff make more errors and a thin department fails in a busy season; and a need for facilities, since staff work better with good training grounds, data tools, and medical equipment that the club business pays for.
items.why: Each of these is part of how real staff succeed or fail.

items.text: Whose judgment sets a club's view of a staff rating: the director of football, the manager's own attributes, or the head of each department.
A contract is negotiated, with a story behind the signature, not filled in as a form.
items.why: A wage and a length typed into a form is the first thing that feels wrong.

items.text: A player weighs more than money when choosing a contract or a club: the role, the manager, the club's project, and life off the pitch.
items.why: A player who counts only the wage is not a person.

items.text: A promise has a cost: when the manager breaks a promise about playing time, a signing, or ambition, the player reacts.
items.why: A free promise is an empty lever.

items.text: The dressing room has structure: leaders, groups, and a pecking order, so unrest can spread and can calm.
items.why: A flat squad cannot carry the mood the board already models.

items.text: A contract carries four groups of parts: money (wage, signing-on fee, loyalty bonus, agent fee), performance bonuses (appearance, goal, clean-sheet, and team success), clauses (release clause, relegation wage cut, promotion rise, option to extend), and promises and status (squad status, playing time, a stated role, and promises about signings or ambition).
items.why: Each part changes a player's choices or a club's money.

items.text: A player's standing in the dressing room comes from four sources: time at the club, ability and fame, a leader's personality, and the captain's armband that the manager gives, where a poor pick loses the squad.
items.why: Real standing comes from all four, and each one gives the manager a different lever.

items.text: Groups form in the squad by language and nation, by age, by starters and bench, and by shared history such as the academy or joining together; a lone new signing can feel shut out.
items.why: Groups are how a grievance or a friendship becomes a squad matter.

items.text: Unrest moves through leaders, who can calm it or spread it; through groups, first inside the player's group and then beyond; into the press, which puts pressure on the manager and the board; and onto the pitch, where a divided squad plays worse together.
items.why: Unrest that stays in one player's mood is not how a real dressing room behaves.

items.text: How much a divided squad plays worse is a design value, because no public match data measures dressing-room division; the value stays below the spread of skill between players.

The manager sees the dressing room three ways at once: some issues show at once, some arrive through people such as the captain and the assistant, and some show only as symptoms whose cause the manager must work out.
items.why: Real managers see the room in part, and each issue reaches them by its own route.

items.text: A divided dressing room has a small effect on the pitch, smaller than the spread of skill between players, so it shows over a season and not in one match.
